item.title: What to Know About Lula’s Election Victory in Brazil, and What Comes Next
item.description:
President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of Brazil won re-election on Sunday, according to official preliminary results, punctuating a string of conservative wins across Latin America. His right-wing opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, refused to accept the outcome.

Mr. Lula became the first presidential candidate since 1989 to win after finishing second in the opening round. In just three weeks, he added more than 10 million votes, gaining ground across the country.

Mr. Lula received 51.8 percent of the vote, compared with 48.2 percent for Mr. Bolsonaro, with nearly all ballots counted. Mr. Bolsonaro called for the election to be annulled after a judge extended voting hours by two hours, a change that both campaigns had requested.

Here’s what to know:

Mr. Lula accomplished what no candidate had done since Brazil restored direct presidential elections in 1989: He won after finishing second in the opening round this month. In each of the nine preceding elections, the first-round leader won the presidency, either outright or in a runoff.

Mr. Lula tried and failed to overcome such a deficit in 1989. After finishing second to Fernando Collor de Mello, he rallied support from defeated rivals and surged in the polls. He ultimately lost in the runoff, 53 percent to 47 percent.

His victory on Sunday added another reversal to an extraordinary political career. Mr. Lula, 80, helped found the Workers’ Party under military rule and lost three presidential elections before winning in 2002. Jailed and barred from running in 2018, he returned to defeat Jair Bolsonaro in 2022 after his corruption convictions were annulled the previous year. He has now won an unprecedented fourth term.

Mr. Lula framed his candidacy as a way to defend democracy, protect Brazil’s sovereignty and prevent the Bolsonaro family’s return to power. Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, promised to restore his father’s conservative agenda while casting himself as a more moderate successor.

The result also halted a regional advance by the right. Although President Trump did not openly champion either candidate in Brazil, as he had in two other elections in Latin America, his administration tried in subtle ways to bolster Mr. Bolsonaro’s campaign.

Mr. Lula, who has repeatedly defied Mr. Trump, said the surge of rallies in the past week “was a demonstration that this country refuses to be anyone’s backyard.” It was an apparent reference to the United States, which has been trying to exert new levels of control over Latin America through measures such as tariffs, sanctions and election intervention.

Mr. Lula’s margin of victory, 3.6 percentage points, was wider than it was four years ago. Few pollsters had predicted his comeback.

At a news conference, Mr. Bolsonaro refused to recognize the result and said he would seek to have the election annulled. He described the court’s decision to extend voting hours as a “dirty trick,” adding, “What happened today was not normal, and it was even unacceptable.”

Both candidates had requested the additional time. Mr. Bolsonaro said that flooding in a part of the country where he had strong support would unfairly hurt him, while Mr. Lula accused public officials of deliberately slowing public transportation in areas where he had won in the first round of voting.

A judge decided minutes before polls closed to extend hours at all polling stations. But by the time of the announcement, some polling centers had already closed and their voting machines had shut down, preventing them from reopening.

To seek to have the election annulled, Mr. Bolsonaro’s party will need to petition the authorities for a review of the results. Since Brazil’s return to democracy, no presidential election has been annulled.

In the 2014 election, the losing party requested an audit, but the review found no evidence of fraud and the results were upheld. In 2022, the Liberal Party similarly challenged Jair Bolsonaro’s election loss but failed to provide evidence to support its accusations and was fined by a court.

Flávio Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party has two possible paths to challenge the result, said Raquel Machado, a professor at the Federal University of Ceará. It could seek a technical audit to determine whether unequal voting conditions affected the outcome, potentially leading to an annulment of the election. Or it could pursue an abuse-of-power case through the Superior Electoral Court’s inspector general, which could disqualify Mr. Lula and his running mate, Geraldo Alckmin, even after they take office.

But Professor Machado noted that many polling stations had closed by the time the Supreme Court’s order was made public and that there had been no significant influx of voters after 5 p.m. local time.

Mr. Lula’s Workers’ Party could bring its own challenge over restrictions on public bus services on Election Day.

item.title: Civilian Suffering Was Goal of Russian Strikes in Ukraine, U.N. Panel Says
item.description:
Russia’s intense and systematic bombardment of Ukraine’s energy infrastructure is intended to inflict harm and suffering on civilians and amounts to a crime against humanity, United Nations investigators said on Monday.

None of the hardships they had endured since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in February 2022 prepared them for the bitter deprivations of last winter, Ukrainians told the three-person Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine.

As temperatures dropped below zero, Russian bombardments involving hundreds of drones and missiles at a time knocked out power generation facilities, cutting off heat, lighting and the power needed to pump water, the investigators’ report said. In the worst-affected areas, millions of people were left without electricity for hours and even days, the Ukrainian authorities told them.

Russia said it had targeted energy infrastructure serving a military use, or a dual one, the commission noted. But the commanders ordering the attacks knew the power generators they were striking were indispensable to local inhabitants and were well aware of the impact, it said.

And the strikes intensified as the temperature dropped — demonstrating “the intent of Russia’s authorities to inflict harm to the civilian population,” the commission said. The report said the attacks had been “widespread and systematic, disproportionate, and amounted to the war crime of excessive incidental death.”

The Ukrainian authorities documented deaths from the cold in homes and even in hospitals, the panel said. And medical workers reported receiving patients suffering from cold-related trauma, including frostbite and hypothermia.

The power cuts took a psychological toll as well. Ukrainians talked of insomnia, exhaustion and depression. One Kyiv resident described struggling to keep awake for fear the cold would kill him in his sleep.

“The scariest thing was to fall asleep and not to wake up,” he told investigators. “It was like torture to be scared of dying from cold.”

Ukraine, too, has attacked energy infrastructure, the panel said, noting reports by the Russian authorities of strikes in Belgorod Oblast and media reports of attacks on energy facilities in Crimea. The investigators said they had been unable to examine those attacks because they lacked access or Russian response to their questions.

Earlier this month, President Trump announced an “energy cease-fire,” with the aim of ending Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries that have reduced supplies of diesel to world markets. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, agreed to halt such attacks if the cease-fire took effect, but Russia’s bombardment of targets across Ukraine continued uninterrupted.

Now it is almost winter once more.

“As the cold season approaches, the attacks have intensified once again, raising serious concerns about the threats to civilians’ lives and health,” said the commission’s chairman, Erik Mose.

The panel also investigated Russia’s treatment of foreign nationals duped into serving with Russian military forces in Ukraine. Some were promised high pay to work as drivers, mechanics or security guards — only to end up on the battlefield.

The investigators found people from 29 countries across Latin America, Africa and Asia they said had been recruited into Russian military service through deception. Most were from poor communities, and a vast majority had no military experience, the report said.

Drawing on the testimony of 245 recruits, the commission found that after arrival in Russia, people had their passports taken and were forced to sign Russian language contracts with the Ministry of Defense committing them to serve a year in the military. Those who refused were physically threatened.

“They took me 100 meters away, shot four Russians in my presence and told me, ‘If you don’t sign, you are the next,’” one former recruit told investigators.

Recruits received military training that varied from 20 minutes to one month before being deployed to frontline units. There, they were forced to dig trenches, collect the bodies or body parts of fallen soldiers, and distribute food and water to troops. They were also used in assaults on enemy positions.

item.title: Israel Has Committed Genocidal Acts in Gaza Since Cease-Fire, U.N. Human Rights Panel Says
item.description:
A commission of United Nations human rights experts said on Monday that Israel was committing genocidal acts against Palestinian civilians in Gaza despite a cease-fire agreement there and carrying out crimes against humanity in the West Bank.

The report by the U.N. Independent Commission of Inquiry, which comes on the eve of Israel’s first general election since the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack, is meant to look at the drivers of violence by Israel and the Palestinian Authority, the panel said. It said that Israel was deliberately targeting Palestinian children and was using torture, rape and sexual violence as part of a broader attack aimed at displacing and subjugating the Palestinian population.

Israel immediately rejected the claims.

The report, delivered to the U.N. General Assembly, noted that between the cease-fire announced on Oct. 10, 2025, and the end of September 2026, Israeli airstrikes, artillery and gunfire had killed 1,431 Palestinians in Gaza, including 300 children. The report rejected a claim in May by the Board of Peace set up by President Trump that the cease-fire had “largely held.”

The combined findings of the U.N. commission, an independent panel of three human rights experts that has already released multiple reports, represent the most authoritative legal analysis of Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza pending a ruling by the International Court of Justice in The Hague on an allegation of genocide filed by South Africa.

“The intentional killing and injuring of Palestinian civilians and destruction of homes in the West Bank combined with Israel’s persistent denial of responsibility form part of a broader strategy to exterminate and displace Palestinians and impose conditions of life that are unlivable,” Srinivasan Muralidhar, an Indian lawyer who serves as the panel’s chairman, said in a statement accompanying the report.

The commission also includes Chris Sidoti, an Australian expert on international human rights law who has served on the panel since it was set up in 2021; and Florence Mumba, a Zambian judge who served on international criminal tribunals investigating war crimes in the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda.

The commission cited a series of Israeli airstrikes, artillery bombardments and sniper attacks in Gaza and said they “show that Israeli authorities and forces continue to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza.”

Israel’s permanent mission to the United Nations in Geneva called the report misinformation and an attempt to demonize Israel.

Daniel Meron, Israel’s ambassador in Geneva, condemned what it called “efforts by actors such as the U.N. Commission of Inquiry to undermine Israel’s legitimacy and deny its fundamental right to exist and defend itself.”

The U.N. panel first asserted that Israel committed genocide in the war in Gaza in September 2025, when the commission was led by Navi Pillay, who was recently awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

The new report said that Israel’s government and security forces had deliberately inflicted death, severe injury and mental harm on Palestinian children, amounting to “age-based persecution.”

It also said that since a report on sexual violence in March 2025, the commission had verified more cases against detainees from Gaza and the West Bank, including gang rape, groping, forced nudity and cavity searches. It also said the commission had investigated two cases of sexual violence against participants in a flotilla of about 50 boats that were apprehended in the Mediterranean Sea as they tried to break Israel’s blockade of Gaza.

The panel said Israeli forces were increasingly applying lethal force against Palestinians in the West Bank, killing 1,080 Palestinians since the cease-fire agreement.

The West Bank has experienced soaring levels of settler violence, but the commission said Israeli security forces were responsible for 95 percent of killings and 82 percent of injuries to Palestinians in this period.

The combination of Israeli military operations and settler violence “had formed part of a widespread and systematic attack against the civilian population in the West Bank,” the panel said, committing war crimes and crimes against humanity.

The targeting of children by security forces and settlers was deliberate and intended to form part of the attack on the civilian population, it said.

Israeli military operations since January 2025 had driven more than 34,000 Palestinians from their homes by August 2026, in what the commission said amounted to the largest displacement of Palestinians in the West Bank since 1967, when Israel captured the territory from Jordan during the Arab-Israeli war that year.

The commission also said that the Palestinian Authority, which administers parts of the Israeli-occupied West Bank, had used excessive force resulting in killings in the course of large-scale operations targeting Palestinians wanted by Israel and conducted in coordination with the Israeli authorities.

Over a period of about two years up to October 2025, such operations had resulted in the deaths of at least 14 Palestinians, the commission reported. The Palestinian Authority responded harshly to criticism of these operations, targeting journalists and human rights defenders in an attempt to silence dissent, it said.

Ibrahim Khraishi, the Palestinian ambassador to the United Nations at Geneva, said in response: “We remain committed to ensuring that law enforcement respects the law and human rights, including freedom of expression and the work of journalists and human rights defenders. Any misconduct will be addressed.”

item.title: Election Surprises
item.description:
It’s officially global election season. Today, Israel votes in what many consider its most important election ever. Next week, the United States holds its midterms, which some voters see as a referendum on the presidency of Donald Trump. (Speaking of which: The New York Times is making its U.S. election coverage free for the next week or so, so download the app here if you want to take advantage of that.)

First, though, let’s talk about Brazil, and about Serbia. There were surprising election results in two very different countries — one big, one small; one in Latin America, the other in the Balkans. But both were a reminder that democracy can produce unexpected results. Today, I write about how voters in Brazil and Serbia defied predictions and what this says about our political moment.

It seemed all but inevitable: Brazil would swerve right, like all the other Latin American countries that held elections in the last 18 months, and elect another Bolsonaro.

Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, was the underdog heading into Sunday’s vote. He was an incumbent in anti-incumbent times. A leftist out of step with an ascendant right. And he was meaningfully behind after the first round of voting earlier this month.

Some 10,000 kilometers northeast, voters in Serbia were also taking part in an election that to many seemed, if not a foregone conclusion, a pretty safe bet.

On the one hand, it was Serbia’s most competitive vote in years, thanks to the student protests over corruption that had been ongoing since 2024. On the other, Serbia’s longtime nationalist strongman, Aleksandar Vucic, had dominated Serbian politics since 2012. He also had a firm grip on the police, nearly all major media outlets and the electoral commission. Surely he would win again.

As it happens, these predictions were most likely also the preferred outcomes of Donald Trump, a Bolsonaro ally, and Vladimir Putin, a Vucic ally.

But as the election results show, voters had other ideas.

High stakes, high turnout

The first rule of comparing election results in two very different countries is that it’s very hard to compare elections in two very different countries. The population of Serbia is smaller than the population of Rio de Janeiro. The elections were focused on different issues. In Serbia, voters effectively kicked out the incumbent; in Brazil, they voted to keep him.

Still, it’s worth pointing out at least one parallel: Both elections had very high voter turnout.

Lula did something that no candidate has done since Brazil restored direct presidential elections in 1989: He won after finishing second in the first round of voting. As my colleagues explain, in each of the nine preceding elections, the first-round leader also won the presidency.

But Lula added more than 10 million votes in between the rounds. He gained support across the country. In the end, he turned a 2-point deficit into an almost 4-point lead. Far more people cast their ballot on Sunday than in the earlier round.

That’s unusual. Normally, the number of voters drops from the first round to the second, my colleagues write. But voters were mobilized by a sense of urgency and high stakes. Lula framed the vote as a fight for Brazilian democracy (his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, is the son of a former president currently in jail for attempting a coup four years ago) and a fight for the country’s sovereignty (Bolsonaro and his father both have a warm relationship with Trump).

Social media seems to have played a role. A wildly popular pro-Lula channel on WhatsApp, a platform long dominated by Bolsonaro’s right-wing movement, helped galvanize Lula’s supporters in the final stretch of the race, my colleagues write. What ultimately mattered, though, is that Brazilian voters cared. In a deeply divisive election, choosing between two very different visions for the future of Latin America’s biggest nation, they turned out to make their voices heard.

The same was true in Serbia. There, too, voters were mobilized by a sense of urgency and stakes.

A Serbian student movement spent the last two years protesting against corruption — the same issues that prompted voters to oust Viktor Orban in nearby Hungary. As the protests swelled, at times drawing as many as 100,000 people, they morphed into calls for Vucic to step down.

Instead, he called a snap election — which he lost resoundingly. Vucic’s party won only about 105 seats in Serbia’s 250-member legislature. The list of candidates selected by the protesting students — professors, scientists, doctors, workers, actors and activists, most of them unknown to the public — won 135.

Not invincible

Another similarity: Both elections also look like losses for the brand of authoritarian-adjacent right-wing populism that, in recent years, has seemed to have so much political momentum behind it. Vucic and Bolsonaro share DNA with, and are allies of, Trump’s MAGA movement.

As my colleague Andrew Higgins, who’s been covering the Serbian elections, points out, in big Western European countries like France or Germany, where far-right populists are now leading in opinion polls, “the anti-establishment nationalist camp has taken on the appearance of an invincible juggernaut” — and its leaders may yet win.

What recent votes in Poland and Hungary, and now Serbia and Brazil, show, however, is that once these parties have actually governed, they, too, can become targets of the voter anger they’re so adept at harnessing, Andrew writes. Even in places where they succeed in tilting the political playing field in their favor, like Serbia, sometimes the anger can become so overwhelming that they still lose.

Just because voters can still deliver election surprises doesn’t mean democracy is healthy in 2026. In Brazil, Flávio Bolsonaro still hasn’t accepted the election results (though his party indicated it would); in Serbia, the process of unwinding Vucic’s grip on state institutions will be long and difficult. But it is a sign that democracy is still alive.

How long can the artificial intelligence boom continue? That’s the crucial question posed by Anthropic as it prepares for a public offering that could value the company at $2 trillion.

Yesterday, the company painted a picture of rapid growth — including coming advances in science and explosive economic expansion — as its revenues increased 14-fold to $16.3 billion in the first half of the year. It is still losing billions of dollars every year.

The entire global economy is arguably riding on upcoming stock market listings of Anthropic and OpenAI. item.title: Mexico’s Top Election Official Resigns Amid Corruption Scandal
item.description:
The head of Mexico’s National Electoral Institute stepped down on Monday amid accusations of corruption, conflict of interest and influence peddling, raising concerns over the credibility of the agency responsible for safeguarding the country’s elections ahead of a major vote next year.

The accusations against Guadalupe Taddei Zavala center on a supposed procurement scheme in which companies linked to a businessman with close ties to her secured lucrative contracts to supply electoral materials to the agency and local election officials.

She is the first president in the electoral watchdog’s history to resign since its creation in 2014.

The leadership shake-up comes as Mexico prepares for a sweeping midterm election next June, when voters will choose officials for more than 20,000 public posts across federal, state and municipal levels, including all 500 seats in the lower house of Congress, 17 governorships and thousands of state and municipal positions.

The vote will be a major test for President Claudia Sheinbaum and her governing Morena party, which holds supermajorities in both chambers of Congress with its allies and controls about three-quarters of the country’s 32 states.

On Monday, Ms. Sheinbaum noted Ms. Taddei’s decision and called for a further investigation into the accusations.

“I think she is making the right decision by stepping aside,” Ms. Sheinbaum said during her daily news conference. “And there can be no allegations, no shadows of corruption, hanging over the electoral institution.”

Ms. Taddei’s resignation comes days after Mexico’s superior audit office — the nation’s top auditing and oversight authority — announced that it had opened an investigation based on irregularities in contracts awarded by the watchdog as well as indications of potential conflict of interests, collusion and diversion of funds, according to a public statement.

The scandal erupted this month after investigative reports revealed close personal ties between Ms. Taddei’s family and the businessman José Alfredo Hernández Casillas, whose network of companies had received hundreds of millions of pesos in electoral agency contracts.

Auditors said they were looking into whether companies coordinated bids to create the appearance of competition while public money was being channeled through intermediary firms with few employees. Investigators are also examining the hiring of some of these companies’ former employees and associates for administrative and technical positions within the electoral agency.

Ms. Taddei, who took over the electoral agency, known as the I.N.E., in 2023, has denied wrongdoing and defended the legality of the appointments. On Sunday, she said she would submit her resignation to Congress on Monday after “profound reflection,” citing the need to protect the agency’s credibility ahead of the upcoming elections.

“This decision reflects my conviction that protecting the institute and allowing it to continue fulfilling its constitutional mission must always take precedence over any short-term or personal interests,” she said in a public statement, adding that her departure did not impede anyone to investigate or clarify any potential wrongdoing.

“Individuals come and go. Institutions endure. Mexican democracy must move forward,” she added.

The controversy deepened on Friday, after a local news outlet released a video purportedly showing one of Ms. Taddei’s sons, Jorge Francisco Piñeda Taddei, and Mr. Hernández, the businessman at the center of the incident, drinking Champagne inside a luxury hotel room in Paris. The footage followed several other news reports documenting Mr. Hernández’s close ties to Ms. Taddei and contracts awarded to companies linked to him.

In a message posted on social media, Ricardo Monreal, a Mexican lawmaker who leads Ms. Sheinbaum’s coalition in Congress and is an influential political figure within Morena, said the lower Chamber of Deputies would call for applications to select a new president of the institute. A technical committee will then review aspiring candidates and elect the next head by a two-thirds majority vote, a process that can take about a month.

The electoral agency’s councilors will meet this week to choose an interim president from among their ranks.

Luis Carlos Ugalde, a political analyst who led the electoral agency from 2003 to 2007, said Ms. Taddei’s resignation came at a critical moment, amid what he described as “democratic backsliding” and growing concerns over the organization’s independence. Opposition parties and analysts have accused some electoral councilors appointed under Morena of favoring the governing party.

The 2027 elections “will test whether Morena can continue expanding its electoral dominance or whether its grip on power will begin to weaken,” he said, helping determine the course of the second half of President Claudia Sheinbaum’s term. “Whoever becomes the next president of the I.N.E. could help restore the institution’s independence and impartiality, or allow it to remain politically captured and continue operating in ways that benefit the ruling party.”

item.title: Netanyahu Pushed for Attack on Iran Ahead of Israeli Election, Officials Say
item.description:
In advance of Israel’s pivotal election on Tuesday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sought for weeks to orchestrate a new airstrike on Iran but ran into resistance from the military’s chief of staff, according to three senior Israeli defense officials and three other people briefed on the matter.

Then, over the past few days, the chief of staff, Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, became concerned that Mr. Netanyahu had begun pushing for a separate action against Iran, short of an overt strike, according to an Israeli official and a person briefed on the matter, neither of whom described the nature of such an action. General Zamir believed that this would be a miscalculation that could provoke Iran into attacking Israel.

Spokesmen for Mr. Netanyahu did not respond immediately to requests for comment.

The Israeli officials and the people briefed on the deliberations spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

Mr. Netanyahu’s rationale for pressing to attack Iran before the election was not clear, but a return to war could have potentially disrupted or even delayed the vote.

The behind-the-scenes tensions over a possible Israeli attack or other action against Iran come as Mr. Netanyahu has been publicly portraying the stakes of the election in increasingly apocalyptic terms. Over the weekend, he posted an A.I.-generated image on social media of a mushroom cloud over Tel Aviv and warned in a television appearance that the vote would decide “Israel’s existence.”

The appeals to Israelis’ fears are meant to get voters to see the conflict with Iran as the most urgent issue and to entrust him with continuing to lead the struggle against Israel’s chief regional adversary.

When Mr. Netanyahu pushed to heat up the conflict with Iran, General Zamir raised a number of objections and concerns and ultimately concluded that there was no immediate or urgent need for action, the officials and people briefed on the matter said.

Such a determination by the military chief carries special weight: It can make it harder to portray the timing as a military necessity.

While General Zamir was not opposed to taking action against Iran in principle, he objected to doing so before the election, according to an Israeli official and two people briefed on the matter. General Zamir and the Israeli air force commander, Maj. Gen. Omer Tischler, cited the political sensitivities and the difficulty of explaining to the public why it had to occur then, according to two senior Israeli defense officials.

In a statement, the Israeli military said its operational decision making was strictly based “on security considerations,” as well as “its responsibility as a national institution.”

The concerns about political motivations for an attack on Iran do not expire on Tuesday. According to three senior Israeli defense officials and two people briefed on the matter, a resumption of fighting with Iran in the weeks after the election could also have a large impact.

If Mr. Netanyahu’s opponents prevail in the election, they would likely have an opportunity to form the new government, but a return to war could hinder or even thwart their ability to assemble a governing coalition within the time allotted by law. Renewed fighting could also create political pressure to establish a national unity government that includes Mr. Netanyahu.

Reports of disagreement between Mr. Netanyahu and the military over a possible attack, first carried by Israel’s Channel 12, sparked outrage in Israel. One of Mr. Netanyahu’s rivals, Avigdor Liberman, demanded Monday that the attorney general open an investigation into whether the prime minister had committed treason.

“The attempt to drag Israel into a war on the eve of elections, including sacrificing Israeli soldiers, just because of the fear of losing the elections, is a betrayal of the nation,” Mr. Liberman, a defense minister and foreign minister in earlier Netanyahu governments, wrote in a formal complaint.

Mr. Netanyahu, 77, is battling to keep his hold on power in the face of opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff.

Mr. Netanyahu’s appeals to voters became increasingly disturbing over the campaign’s final weekend, with the prime minister saying that his defeat could lead to Israel’s annihilation. He has also suggested that tougher times could be ahead for Israel regardless of the outcome.

On Friday, he said that Israelis should prepare for the end of billions of dollars in American military support from the United States, given the sharp decline of Israel’s standing in U.S. public opinion. He also said the possibility that Israel will face “banking sanctions” arising from international condemnation could force the country in coming years to rely on cryptocurrency to circumvent the penalties.

The remarks prompted a wave of criticism. Israel’s nonpartisan central bank, the Bank of Israel, issued a rare warning, saying that cryptocurrency would not save the economy in the event of international sanctions. And a former governor of the Bank of Israel, Jacob Frenkel, said that turning away from the global financial system would make Israel into “a leper.”

Opposition leaders accused Mr. Netanyahu of essentially accepting that Israel would become a pariah state.

“He’s lost it,” said Yair Lapid, one of Mr. Netanyahu’s centrist rivals. “Israel’s prime minister, in an election campaign, is saying three days before the elections to vote for him and he’ll ensure that Israel stays isolated.”

For weeks, Mr. Netanyahu has also been saying that Iran might attack Israel in an attempt to sabotage the elections — statements that some military analysts consider destabilizing. His messaging became even more dire over the weekend.

On Sunday morning, Mr. Netanyahu posted the image of an A.I.-generated cloud from a nuclear blast mushrooming over Tel Aviv, Israel’s biggest metropolis. He attached a quote from a supporter to the effect that the scandals dogging him — he is currently facing trial on corruption charges, which he denies — were a distraction from “the real and tangible existential danger” that Iran posed.

Iran denies that it is pursuing a nuclear weapon but has also repeatedly threatened Israel, which is widely believed to have its own nuclear arsenal.

Hours later, Mr. Netanyahu gave one of the final interviews of his election campaign to Israel’s Channel 14, a network that largely echoes the prime minister’s talking points. He warned that his right-wing bloc was facing possible defeat.

“It’s not in our pocket and it’s not a lost cause,” Mr. Netanyahu said.

The prime minister warned that Israel was at risk of joining the ranks of countries like Belgium, Britain and France that, he said, have been “ruined” by an alliance between “the left and radical Islam.”

Rising to his feet, Mr. Netanyahu likened himself to a Jewish leader warning 1930s European Jewry of the impending Holocaust. Mr. Netanyahu said Mr. Eisenkot and his allies would not do what was necessary and vowed to destroy Iran’s nuclear program and topple its government.

Mr. Netanyahu has repeatedly boasted of having destroyed the Iranian nuclear program, only to speak of it as if it remains an imminent threat. “We cannot live side by side with this bomb,” he said. “Either they will either destroy us or we will destroy that poisonous cult.”

Mr. Netanyahu’s opponents also believe the future of their country is hanging in the balance on Tuesday. Many liberal Israelis fear that this election is their last chance to prevent their country from becoming an authoritarian state, under the sway of the religious right and shunned on the world stage.

On Sunday evening, Mr. Eisenkot made his own final pitch to voters, calling for the country to come together “to save our Israel.” He vowed to order an inquiry into the government’s failure to prevent the Hamas-led attack against Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, uproot Hamas’s rule in Gaza within 18 months and force Mr. Netanyahu’s ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies, now exempted from military service, to share the burden of conscription.

“At stake in the elections is nothing less than the security of Israel and the survival of the Israeli story as we know it,” Mr. Eisenkot said.

item.title: The Digital Army That Catapulted Lula to Victory in Brazil
item.description:
It started with a WhatsApp channel with a few thousand followers. It exploded into a digital army of 10 million people that helped swing Latin America’s biggest election.

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of Brazil staged a stunning comeback on Sunday, achieving an unexpected victory over Flávio Bolsonaro, the right-wing challenger whose father tried to stage a coup after losing the last election.

In winning, Mr. Lula did what no other presidential candidate has accomplished in Brazil’s history — he won election after finishing second in the first round.

His victory rested, to a significant degree, on social media. A tidal wave of messages, memes and reels flooded Brazil, a chronically online nation of 214 million, and rallied millions of Brazilians with diverging views around a single task: barring the return of the Bolsonaro family to power.

Mr. Lula’s win delivered a powerful rebuke to a right-wing movement barreling through Latin America that has been applauded by President Trump. It also deals a blow to Washington’s plans for economic and military dominance in the region, extending the reign of the only leader in Latin America — and one of the few globally — who has defied Mr. Trump.

Mr. Lula won by about double the margin he achieved in 2022, when he narrowly defeated Mr. Bolsonaro’s father, Jair Bolsonaro. The achievement is all the more remarkable because Mr. Lula, who entered the race as the underdog, received more than 10 million votes between the first and second rounds of the election, or roughly three out of every four new votes up for grabs on Sunday. The younger Mr. Bolsonaro captured roughly four million additional votes than he did in the first round.

“It was a very big victory for global democracy,” said Christian Lynch, a political scientist at Rio de Janeiro State University. It was driven, he said, by an unprecedented mobilization of Brazilian voters. “We never saw anything like this.”

These votes came from some unexpected sources.

For one, nine million people voted for minor conservative candidates in the first round. Analysts believe a significant slice of those votes went to Mr. Lula rather than the younger Mr. Bolsonaro, defying predictions ahead of the vote.

This suggested that the Bolsonaro family’s brand of right-wing politics had ultimately failed to convince some moderate conservatives.

“I’m much more of a right-wing guy — but not the far right that exists now,” said Leandro Cantini Lopes, 38, a restaurant consultant in Rio de Janeiro, who voted for Mr. Lula on Sunday after supporting a moderate conservative earlier.

Turnout also increased by nearly three million between the first and second rounds, a highly unusual reversal in a country where absenteeism tends to rise after the initial vote. Absenteeism fell to the lowest level of any Brazilian presidential election — another sign that Mr. Lula had succeeded in motivating supporters to turn out in big numbers.

Some voters were likely spooked into voting by just how much power Mr. Bolsonaro may have had as president, analysts said. With his political party making major strides in the legislature, he would have faced a mostly clear path to rewriting Brazil’s past and reshaping its future.

The elder Mr. Bolsonaro last year was sentenced to 27 years in prison for trying to stage a coup after losing the last election to Mr. Lula. His son has vowed to seek his amnesty and impeach the justices who jailed him.

Felipe Haurelhuk, 41, started worrying when the younger Mr. Bolsonaro, triumphant after his first-round victory, began talking about rewriting Brazil’s Constitution with the help of his political allies. He decided to cast a ballot for Mr. Lula, after voting for a different conservative candidate earlier this month.

“Terrible for democracy,” Mr. Haurelhuk, who owns a beauty salon in São Paulo, said referring to a potential Bolsonaro victory. “Brazil will keep moving somewhat sideways” under Mr. Lula, he added. “But better that than handling power over to the Bolsonaro camp.”

Just three weeks ago, a triumph for Mr. Lula seemed unfathomable. He had finished 2.2 million votes behind Mr. Bolsonaro in the first round of voting, with analysts declaring him on the cusp of defeat.

Then, a charismatic leftist lawmaker from one of Brazil’s most populous states made a fateful rallying cry on a WhatsApp channel. At 6 a.m. the day after Mr. Lula’s defeat in the first round, André Janones, the lawmaker, called on his 53,000 followers to get to work. He renamed the channel Lula’s Army.

Around the clock, Mr. Janones, in the persona of a digital drill sergeant, would issue “missions” to the swelling number of followers in the channel. Over the next five days, the group grew to 3.4 million.

“Urgent!” he shouted in video and audio messages, ordering supporters to comment, like and share posts favoring Mr. Lula on social media. “Go viral!”

The online frenzy to re-elect Mr. Lula only grew after accusations by his campaign and independent watchdogs that Meta, which owns WhatsApp, was favoring his right-wing rival on its platforms. To try to sidestep the algorithm, Mr. Janones and his followers began filming videos wearing Brazil’s yellow jersey — a symbol of the right — and using online tactics usually employed by Mr. Bolsonaro’s movement to increase its reach.

The channel, and its head-spinning growth, drew the attention of Mr. Bolsonaro and the electoral court. After a judicial arm wrestle between justices on the electoral court, the channel was allowed to stay up. But the court’s chief justice, who was appointed by the elder Mr. Bolsonaro, ordered Meta to investigate how it had grown so much. Meta found no irregularities.

Online, Mr. Lula’s army of supporters seized on corruption investigations swirling around the younger Mr. Bolsonaro, who has not been charged with a crime. They questioned his past links to figures from Rio’s criminal underworld and his father’s handling of the pandemic. And they warned about the risks of his vague plans to cut public spending, inspired by the austerity measures applied by President Javier Milei of Argentina.

“This channel will not spread a single piece of fake news,” Mr. Janones ordered his followers. “Those who have the facts have no need for lies!”

Mr. Janones’s channel grew exponentially, eventually hitting 10 million subscribers. And just days before the vote, it welcomed a high-profile new member: Mr. Lula finally got his first smartphone and joined the channel.

“This was a 20th-century man who, at the very last possible moment, figured out how to run a 21st-century campaign,” Brian Winter, an American political analyst who studies Latin America, said of Mr. Lula.

The digital push spilled out into the real world, igniting mass demonstrations. And it helped win over some voters, like Marina Dalla Líbera Pedro, who drove for two days, with her children, to cast a ballot for Mr. Lula on Sunday, after skipping the first round. “I had to defend our rights,” said Ms. Pedro, 40, an engineer in Rio das Ostras, a small coastal city 100 miles from Rio de Janeiro. “I saw it as a collapse of society.”

Yet Mr. Lula’s stunning victory capped a chaotic race that has divided Brazil and risks further eroding faith in its institutions.

Polls were ordered to remain open after public transportation delays and torrential rains disrupted voting. The extended polling hours, which both candidates asked for but came right as voting was set to conclude, led Mr. Bolsonaro on Monday to say he planned to legally challenge the outcome.

Mr. Bolsonaro called an order by Brazil’s judiciary to extend voting a “dirty trick.”

Mr. Trump also criticized the vote. “It looked terrible,” he told reporters at an event in Maryland. “I mean, I didn’t take sides, but it looked like another rigged election.”

Only a small fraction of the votes — 0.03 percent — were cast after regular voting hours, and the chief justice of the electoral authority said keeping polls open did not make a difference in the result, which saw Mr. Lula win by a notable margin.

Still, Mr. Bolsonaro’s complaints, coupled with the confusion marking the last hours of voting, are likely to feed unfounded suspicions about the safety of the Brazilian voting systems.

International experts agree Brazil’s electronic voting machines, a frequent target of misinformation attempts by Mr. Bolsonaro’s movement, are some of the most secure in the world. Yet a poll shows 34 percent of Brazilians distrust the voting machines, up from 20 percent in 2022.

While in office, the elder Mr. Bolsonaro cast unfounded doubts about electoral fraud and claimed he could lose only if the vote were stolen. After his defeat, these claims inspired supporters to assault government buildings, demanding the military overturn the election result.

Reporting was contributed by Sergio Peçanha in Washington, Silvia Ribeiro, Isabela Cruz and Lis Moriconi in Rio de Janeiro.

item.title: France Makes Concessions to Students, but Not Enough to Halt Protests
item.description:
The French government announced on Monday that it would phase out an unpopular online university admissions platform, a significant concession to high school students who have led a protest movement that has mushroomed into weeks of nationwide unrest.

The measure, one of several announced by the education ministry, did not mollify the students. Leaders of high school and university student groups called on them to protest again on Oct. 31 and Nov. 5, even after meeting with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu and hearing the proposals.

Still, the concessions showed that the government was trying to respond to the complaints of students. Many of them criticize the admissions platform, known as Parcoursup, as being opaque and unfair. The government said it would revise the system in 2027 to make it more transparent, and replace it in 2028.

The government also said it would create 15,000 new higher education spaces for students, cap the size of second-year high school classes at 28 students and make available four billion euros ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate dilapidated middle school and high school buildings.

“None of the decisions we make are empty promises,” the education minister, Édouard Geffray, said at a news conference. “Everything we say will be done and respected within specific time frames and with figures.”

The government’s capacity to respond to the students is constrained because of its dire public finances. With widening fiscal deficits, it simply does not have billions of additional euros to spend on schools. But the decision to overhaul and then replace the university admissions platform was welcomed, even if student leaders said it was not enough to end their protests.

“We are managing to achieve some gains through mobilization, but they are still crumbs,” Sabrine Kharbach, a representative of one of the groups, the Student Union, said to the news agency Agence France-Presse.

Louis Letoublon, the vice president of another student group, Les Lycéens!, told reporters after the meeting with Mr. Lecornu, “We can say that we’ve gained something: first, the government’s fear.”

High school students have complained about overcrowded classrooms, a shortage of teachers and crumbling facilities. Among their demands are major investments to upgrade facilities and enough spaces in universities so that every high school graduate is guaranteed a spot.

They erected barricades in front of schools, sometimes clashing with the police. And as their movement grew, it drew in protesters unhappy about high fuel prices and France’s slow-growing economy.

On Oct. 17, a day of mass protests devolved into widespread arson, looting and other violence, putting the government on the defensive. While there were more clashes between protesters and the police at the end of demonstrations this past Saturday, the authorities managed to avert a repeat of the lawlessness that engulfed French cities the previous week.

President Emmanuel Macron, who traveled to Marseille on Monday to meet shop owners, police officers and public officials, said he was ready to take actions that would respond to the “legitimate demands at the root of the social movement.”

item.title: Venezuelan Opposition Leader’s Return Tests Limits of U.S. Sway
item.description:
The return of Venezuela’s top opposition leader, María Corina Machado, after nearly a year in exile is a significant turning point in the Trump administration’s efforts to micromanage the politics of the oil-rich country.

Until Ms. Machado surfaced over the weekend before adulating crowds, Trump officials had prioritized an alignment with her rival, Delcy Rodríguez, a figure from Venezuela’s authoritarian government chosen by the U.S. administration as the country’s leader.

But Ms. Machado’s sudden return is now shifting the political calculus of everything from the Trump administration’s pursuit of opaque oil deals in Venezuela to demands that the U.S. government accelerate a glacially paced transition to democracy.

“Delcy derives her legitimacy solely from the White House, whereas Maria Corina derives hers from the Venezuelan people,” said James B. Story, the U.S. ambassador to Venezuela from 2018 to 2023.

Now that Ms. Machado is back on the ground, pressure is building to speed up what Mr. Story called the Venezuelan government’s “milquetoast” approach for gradually easing authoritarian rule, without a detailed plan for presidential elections.

For months, Trump administration officials had viewed a return by Ms. Machado as potentially disruptive and had intervened earlier to keep that from happening, U.S. officials said. But the United States did not try to block her latest effort, nor did it help.

A spokesman for Ms. Machado said her return was carried out strictly by Venezuelans from the opposition leader’s team.

Ms. Machado’s capacity for energizing Venezuela’s opposition was vividly on display on Sunday as thousands of her followers lined up to cheer her motorcade as it made its way to the capital, Caracas.

Karla Gómez, 54, a registered nurse who was among the throngs of supporters, said she was so overcome with emotion that she cried when she found out Ms. Machado had returned.

“I know it won’t be easy because we’re living under a regime,” said Ms. Gómez, referring to Venezuela’s government, which stifled dissent after losing a 2024 election. “But I know she’ll bring about the changes we desperately need.”

Reflecting the Venezuelan government’s unease with this turn of events, Ms. Rodríguez, the interim president, said on Monday that Ms. Machado had staged a “show” to highlight her return and could have been simply been welcomed at an airport like other returning exiles.

Ms. Rodríguez, who has been praised repeatedly by President Trump, also declined to say whether she would welcome Ms. Machado in talks aimed at renewing democratic institutions.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Monday told reporters in Washington that he expected Ms. Rodríguez and her government to comply with the road map that the United States is presenting for what he and his aides call a gradual political transition.

“What if they just try to wait us out for two years?” he said, an apparent reference to the end of Mr. Trump’s term. “That’s not going to happen. I mean, we have timelines that are agreed to, and so far they’ve met every one of those timelines.”

He added that the United States has kept many economic sanctions on Venezuela — though it issues licenses to companies as exceptions to those — and that the sanctions give the Trump administration “significant influence” over the direction of the ongoing political talks.

That dialogue, intended to put in place a framework for elections, is led on the opposition side by Dinorah Figuera, a member of the legislature elected in 2015 that is formally recognized by the United States. The government side is led by Jorge Rodríguez, the brother of Ms. Rodríguez and head of the current legislature.

Ms. Machado has not been part of the talks, and it is unclear what role she might play.

The fourth round of talks is scheduled for mid-November, and the planning for that could prove to be a test of how Ms. Machado works with other opposition leaders and whether she sees the dialogue as legitimate.

The State Department under Mr. Rubio, who is essentially running Venezuela, envisions two major steps taking place before fair elections can occur. First, a committee of experts must name new members to the Supreme Court, which can wield power over elections. Second, a separate committee must name new members of the National Electoral Council, which administers elections.

The new Supreme Court members could be in place by the end of this year, and the new electoral council could soon follow, a senior State Department official said on Monday. After that, he said, Ms. Rodríguez would declare a permanent vacancy in the presidency, since the country’s last official leader — Nicolás Maduro — is in an American prison, and that would by law trigger a six-month deadline for holding elections.

Ms. Machado has called for elections by next July.

Mr. Trump has lauded Ms. Rodríguez and said Venezuela is not ready for elections. He rarely talks about democracy, openly admires autocrats and tried to overturn the results of the 2020 U.S. presidential election.

But Mr. Rubio insisted the administration supports real democracy in Venezuela: “Our goal here is to have an election that, when it happens, the losing side will say it was a fair election. We just lost. We’ll go into opposition, and when you guys screw up the country, we’ll run in four years and retake power.”

Mr. Rubio, who is also Mr. Trump’s national security adviser, said the “best case scenario” is he stays in his job until the end of the administration and sees Venezuela become a democracy “well in advance” of leaving his position or positions.

Ms. Machado was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2025 and left Venezuela in December to receive the prize in Norway. A month later, U.S. forces overthrew Mr. Maduro, the country’s longtime leader, in a lethal nighttime assault.

But instead of siding with Ms. Machado, who mobilized broad support in her 2024 bid for the presidency, the Trump administration settled on Ms. Rodríguez, who pivoted overnight from unelected adversary to subserviently working with U.S. officials.

Ms. Machado then found herself shut out from negotiations purportedly aimed at setting the stage for a democratic transition. As Ms. Machado remained outside Venezuela, Trump officials focused on deals to revive the country’s oil industry.

One of those deals involves a partnership to produce oil between the U.S. government and Alejandro Betancourt, a Venezuelan businessman who has faced money laundering investigations.

Reflecting unease in Venezuela over the deal, Ms. Machado, in an interview this month with The New York Times, criticized Mr. Betancourt.

Mr. Betancourt has rejected Ms. Machado’s criticism, and his representatives have repeatedly said that he has not been charged with any crimes.

Asked on Monday about Ms. Machado’s criticisms, Mr. Rubio defended the oil deal with Mr. Betancourt. “It now allows the company that we partnered with to go out and make massive capital investments to increase the productive capacity,” he said.

“As far as her criticism of the deal, I mean, that’s fine, I mean, that’s her opinion on it,” he added. “This is a contract that we think is a very solid contract.”

One of Ms. Machado’s immediate challenges will involve fending off attacks from the right. Valentina Gómez, a MAGA firebrand who has lost elections in Missouri and Texas, recently surfaced in Venezuela to express support for Mr. Betancourt’s oil company while excoriating Ms. Machado.

With the U.S. government currently exerting extraordinary control over Venezuela’s oil exports and its government, Ms. Machado is aware that she must tread carefully to avoid offending the Trump administration while also asserting her own leadership.

Rafael Uzcátegui, director of the Peace Laboratory, a Caracas human rights group, argued on social media that Ms. Machado’s presence in the country could open the way for Venezuelans who have avoided publicly criticizing the Trump-Delcy alignment to start doing so.

“Her return creates a credible opening to challenge U.S. tutelage,” Mr. Uzcátegui said.

Anatoly Kurmanaev and María Victoria Fermín contributed reporting from Caracas, Venezuela.

item.title: Flávio Bolsonaro Ordered to Hand Over Passport in Money Laundering Inquiry
item.description:
Brazil’s Supreme Court on Monday ordered the police to seize the passport of Flávio Bolsonaro, the presidential candidate defeated in Sunday’s election, because he is under criminal investigation related to a money laundering scheme.

The ruling, issued by Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, stems from an inquiry into Mr. Bolsonaro’s links to a Brazilian lawyer who is accused of laundering more than $1 billion through a vast fraud scheme, according to a court document reviewed by The New York Times.

Mr. Bolsonaro, a right-wing senator, came on the radar of the authorities when the police said earlier this month that they had discovered that Mr. Bolsonaro had access to the bank accounts of a company owned by the lawyer, Willer Tomaz. In May 2025, a person employed by the lawyer asked the bank to revoke the senator’s access to the accounts, according to a Federal Police report reviewed by the Times.

The ruling also ordered Mr. Bolsonaro to stay away from Mr. Tomaz, a close friend of the right-wing senator. Mr. Tomaz has denied any wrongdoing and rejected claims that Mr. Bolsonaro managed his company’s account.

Mr. Bolsonaro has brushed off the investigation, denying having done any business with Mr. Tomaz and casting the case as political persecution. On Monday, he again framed the confiscation of his travel documents as an attempt to intimidate him following his loss at the polls, which he is disputing.

Mr. Bolsonaro, in a statement, said he would comply and turn over his documents, but insisted that he had “never considered” leaving Brazil. His brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, had suggested on a podcast that, if the candidate were to lose, he should leave Brazil.

Days before the election, Mr. Tomaz traveled to the United States, according to the federal police.

In a separate case, Mr. Bolsonaro is also under investigation over millions of dollars he raised from a disgraced banker at the center of a massive corruption scheme to fund a biopic about his jailed father.

Mr. Bolsonaro’s father, Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence for trying to stage a coup following the last presidential election.

This is not the first time Justice Moraes has collided with the Bolsonaros. Last year, the justice oversaw Mr. Bolsonaro’s trial on the coup charges.

That plot, according to prosecutorial evidence, included plans to assassinate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who was the president-elect at the time and is now president, and Justice Moraes himself. Jair Bolsonaro was sentenced by a five-member panel of justices to 27 years in prison, which he is serving at home because of poor health.

Earlier this year, a panel of Supreme Court justices also convicted and sentenced Eduardo Bolsonaro for seeking to have the Trump administration interfere in his father’s trial.

Eduardo Bolsonaro, who has been living in Texas since early 2025, lobbied the Trump administration to pressure Mr. Lula’s government, through tariffs and sanctions, to drop its case against his father.

One of the targets of those sanctions was Justice Moraes, whom the right has accused of silencing conservative voices through his rulings on online posts. Justice Moraes’s work involving online disinformation has turned him into a hero and villain in a complicated global debate over the limits of online speech.

After the Jair Bolsonaro was convicted, the U.S. sanctions against Justice Moraes were dropped. But in recent months, Eduardo Bolsonaro and allies in the United States have been lobbying the Trump administration to reinstate them.

Underscoring the cloud of corruption that hangs over Brazil’s ruling establishment, Justice Moraes faces his own links to one of the same scandals dogging Mr. Bolsonaro.

A police dossier suggested that Justice Moraes may have exchanged dozens of messages with the disgraced banker, Daniel Vorcaro.

In texts apparently sent to Justice Moraes, Mr. Vorcaro asked for help avoiding arrest. In other exchanges with associates, Mr. Vorcaro mentioned paying millions to a law firm run by the justice’s wife. Justice Moraes has denied wrongdoing.

item.title: A Rare Cease-Fire, Brokered by Melania Trump, Begins in a Besieged Ukrainian City
item.description:
A rare local cease-fire in Ukraine took effect early Tuesday morning to allow aid delivery and evacuation in a Russian-occupied frontline city where about 2,000 civilians are trapped, threatened by starvation and constant bombardment.

The plight of the city, Oleshky, has drawn international attention. Melania Trump announced the local truce on Friday after negotiation with both the Russian and Ukrainian governments. A week earlier, Pope Leo XIV, just three days after surgery for lung cancer, spoke with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia and called for a cease-fire to enable an evacuation there.

Ukrainian officials, volunteers and relatives of people in Oleshky joined a frenzy of messages, calls and announcements to organize residents to register for transport out of the city.

“Every three minutes, people message and call me about evacuation,” said Ksenia Arkhipova, a Ukrainian volunteer worker from Oleshky who has been helping with coordination plans from elsewhere in Ukraine.

People were asking her if many others had signed up for the evacuation, and when she said they had, they asked to join, too, she said. By midday Monday, she said she had gathered 200 names on a list and had some 300 more people she wanted to contact.

“They gave us so little time,” she said of the Friday announcement.

Oleshky sits on the southeastern bank of the Dnipro river in southern Ukraine, where the river forms the front between the warring armies. It has been under Russian occupation since the full-scale invasion of 2022.

On the opposite bank of the river is the much larger city of Kherson, which fell to Russia but was later retaken by Ukrainian forces.

About 24,000 people lived in Oleshky at the time of the invasion, but most of them fled early on.

Yuri Sobolevsky, deputy chairman of the Kherson regional council, the local Ukrainian governing body, said many of those who remained were older people.

“In most cases, people don’t leave because it’s their home, and they will stay despite any circumstances and wait for better times,” he said.

But the civilian population has dwindled as things worsened in Oleshky.

“It’s hell there,” Mr. Sobolevsky said. “People need to be evacuated from there, one thousand percent. They’re living 24/7 under risk of death.”

With the rising dominance of drones in this war, Oleshky falls squarely in the widening “kill zone” between the two sides, largely abandoned by civilians, where anything that moves on the ground can be seen from above as a target.

This year, that drone warfare has grown markedly more intense. Russian soldiers and drone pilots operate out of ruined buildings in Oleshky, using it as a base to strike Kherson, on the northwest bank. Kherson, where more than 40,000 people live, is hit daily by drones and bombs.

Ukrainian drone pilots, in turn, try to defend Kherson by hitting the Russian military in Oleshky.

“It’s the constant accumulation of drones on both sides,” said Roman Kostenko, a member of Ukraine’s Parliament and secretary of the defense and intelligence committee. “The intensity of combat operations has grown due to the fact that there are more drones, more crews, and the enemy has set a goal to destroy Kherson.”

“So many apartment buildings in Oleshky are used for positions to strike Kherson,” he said.

“Of course, then it’s a two-way battle,” he added. “Kherson is also under increased attack since the spring. Therefore, in response, our defense forces are also trying to destroy the enemy.”

In addition, most roads in and out of the city have been mined and traffic is targeted by drones. Trucks stopped delivering food and medicine to Oleshky months ago because the drive was too dangerous. Many people have lost electricity, heat and gas service.

A Ukrainian drone operator working in the area said pilots took pains to distinguish between civilians and soldiers.

“If surveillance sees a person in a uniform, we strike,” said the pilot, who asked to be identified only by a call sign, Dragon, for security and in accordance with military protocol. “If we find a house with people in uniform, we knock it down.”

The cease-fire began at 3 a.m. Tuesday in Ukraine (9 p.m. Monday in the eastern United States), but the evacuation cannot begin right away.

The first task will be mine clearance of access roads by Russian engineers, followed by the trucking in of humanitarian aid, including medicines and food, to the city. People will then be registered for evacuation and are expected to leave on a convoy of buses starting on Thursday.

Russia and Ukraine have blamed each other for turning Oleshky into a death trap, and both are trying to dominate the public relations around the evacuation.

Yana Lantratova, Russia’s human rights commissioner, said in a statement on Monday that a Russian mission to Oleshky would learn the needs of the people there and deliver aid.

“Another task is to ensure the departure of people who, I emphasize, will voluntarily make such a decision,” she said.

She added, “there are not many people in Oleshky who have expressed a desire to leave.”

The agreed route for the evacuation is through Russian-held territory, so only Russian forces will be involved. Ukrainian officials are concerned that Russia will present the event as a grand humanitarian gesture by Moscow.

They have also warned that the civilians feared that they would be arrested or harassed by the Russians, or that Russia would make it difficult for them to return to Ukrainian-held territory.

As long as Russia keeps bombarding Kherson, Oleshky will remain strategically important to it.

The Ukrainian drone pilot said, “If we want Kherson to live, not one building should remain standing in Oleshky.”

“People should leave,” the pilot said. “They should leave, and not return.”

Mr. Kostenko, the Ukrainian Parliament member, said there were concerns that a cease-fire would allow the Russian military to resupply and rotate its troops there, including some who have positions on islands in the Dnipro delta. Some Russian soldiers had even attempted a river crossing to Kherson several weeks ago, he said.

“We understand the enemy will use this to his advantage,” he said. “I think they will try to do a rotation, bring in more forces, regroup, take better positions. So we will need to watch them.”

Siobhán O’Grady and Liubov Sholudko contributed reporting from Kyiv. Andrew E. Kramer contributed reporting.

item.title: King Charles’s Caribbean Tour Is a High-Stakes Diplomatic Test
item.description:
King Charles III has already proved he can deftly navigate tricky diplomatic missions.

During a state visit to America in April, he charmed President Trump even as he subtly pushed back against the worldview of a man who is wildly unpopular among most of his own subjects back in Britain.

This week, the British monarch faces a perhaps even more vexing challenge. How to hold together the Commonwealth, the loosely bound remnants of an empire his ancestors once ruled, amid demands to apologize for colonialism and pay reparations for those who were not only subjects of the realm, but subjected to the evils of slavery?

In a seven-day trip to the Caribbean that begins on Tuesday, the king will visit three countries and then convene the leaders of 56 member nations of the Commonwealth. It is a largely symbolic voluntary group consisting mostly of onetime British colonies; some still also regard him as their ceremonial head of state but many are now republics. There, he will confront renewed calls, including from the organization’s secretary-general, for a frank discussion about those difficult issues.

“We are calling for a dialogue of decency,” Hilary Beckles, the chairman of the Reparations Commission for CARICOM, an organization of Caribbean states, told reporters last week during a briefing ahead of the king’s visit.

“I’m appealing to Charles Windsor, a parent, a grandparent,” Mr. Beckles, the vice chancellor of the University of the West Indies, said. “He can see the enrichment that slavery has presented to his family. He can see that the wealth he’s passing on to his children and his grandchildren all came out as significant sums to this process of the chatilization of the African people.”

Ed Owens, a historian who writes about the British monarchy, said that the king’s visit to the Caribbean was inherently fraught because of the legacy of colonialism and exploitation there. About three million enslaved Africans were trafficked on British ships across the Atlantic in the 1700s and 1800s to work on colonial plantations. Attempted rebellions were brutally crushed.

“The dominion of Britain and the white power over those peoples of color” in centuries past still looms over the monarchy, Mr. Owens said. “The whiteness of the institution is the problem. It remains an emblem of British white supremacy.”

Buckingham Palace said in a statement that Charles, 77, would not seek to avoid the subject of “the darkest days of our past.” But he would not apologize, in line with his constitutional role, which prevents him from diverging from official government policy. The statement said the issue of reparations was the responsibility of Britain’s government.

For Charles, who as a prince said that the “appalling atrocity of slavery” was one that “forever stains our history,” the visit to the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda is another test of his ability to shine on the world stage.

For decades, it was his mother, Queen Elizabeth II, who was the face of the waning British Empire, which came to an end during her reign, and then of the Commonwealth. After his coronation in 2023 at the age of 73, Charles finally emerged from the royal scandals that have plagued his family and has become a global diplomat of sorts, including by using his role to offer support for Ukraine and Canada.

So far, he has surprised some royal watchers.

“He’s proved to be a very effective constitutional monarch,” said Philip Murphy, the director of history and policy at the University of London’s Institute of Historical Research.

“He can deliver a speech very well,” added Mr. Murphy, who is the former head of the Institute of Commonwealth Studies. “And he can deliver it with a degree of personal conviction and humor that his mother, you know, singularly lacked.”

The king deployed both attributes during his visit to the United States this year. During a speech to Congress, he prompted bipartisan laughter with his line about the commonalities between America and Britain. “Everything in common,” he said, “except of course language.”

At the White House state dinner, he stroked Mr. Trump’s ego by giving him a brass bell from a World War II-era British submarine, emblazoned with the sub’s name: H.M.S. Trump. The king also tweaked the president for his “readjustments to the East Wing,” saying that he was sorry for his ancestors’ “own small attempt at real estate redevelopment of the White House” when the British set it on fire in 1814.

“What he did there very cannily was reinvigorate British and American ties by carefully working around a very difficult president,” Mr. Owens said. “Charming him, but also challenging him.”

Humorous moments might be harder to come by in the week ahead, as King Charles and Queen Camilla try to avoid the kind of public relations disaster that befell Prince William and Catherine, the Princess of Wales, in the Caribbean several years ago.

Their weeklong visit to Belize, Jamaica and the Bahamas in 2022 was supposed to be a celebration of Queen Elizabeth’s jubilee. Instead, they heard calls for reparations, plans to become a republic and protests over a land dispute. In one infamous moment, the two were photographed shaking hands with Jamaican children through a chain-link fence.

Those are the kinds of images the palace will be hoping to avoid for Charles and Camilla. There will be stops at sporting events, educational institutions and several demonstrations of environmental projects, long a priority for the king.

Last week, Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey, the secretary-general of the Commonwealth and Ghana’s former foreign minister, said that “the time has come” to discuss whether Britain should pay reparations to the descendants of British slaves. She added that an apology from the king “wouldn’t hurt at all.”

“I don’t believe we can run away from it,” she told Sky News. “But it is important to determine the form that reparations should take, and that is something that will emerge eventually as countries sit around the table to discuss — as difficult a subject as it is, I believe that countries will come to some conclusions.”

David Comissiong, the ambassador of Barbados to CARICOM, said in the briefing for reporters that “by addressing the still existing negative effects of that monumental crime, we will usher in not only an era of reparative justice, but what we are now calling the coming enlightenment.”

Ben Judah, who served as a top adviser to David Lammy when he was Britain’s foreign secretary last year, said last week that the organization needed to be restructured.

“It is time to admit that the Commonwealth does not only not serve its purpose, but works against its premise of post-imperial comity,” Mr. Judah wrote on social media. “This is because it has become a little more than a poorly attended biannual summit whose only purpose seems to be to for Caribbean countries to lobby Britain for reparations. This does nothing but worsen these relationships.”

Of the 56 members of the Commonwealth, only 14 besides Britain remain part of Charles’s realm, with him as their ceremonial head of state. (Australia, New Zealand and Canada are the largest of those.) The rest have shifted to a republican form of government.

In Antigua and Barbuda, where the Commonwealth meeting will be held, Prime Minister Gaston Browne said in 2022 that the country would hold a referendum on leaving the realm. The vote has yet to take place.

It will be up to King Charles to make the case for staying in the realm, and — more broadly — for the future of the Commonwealth as an institution, more than seven decades after its creation.

item.title: What’s the Commonwealth? A Guide as King Charles Heads to the Caribbean.
item.description:
King Charles and Queen Camilla of Britain are traveling to the Caribbean this week. There, the king will bring together the leaders of more than 50 nations for the biennial meeting of an organization known as the Commonwealth.

But what is the Commonwealth? How did it get started? Who are its members? And what does it do?

Here’s what to know:

The Commonwealth of Nations was born during the disintegration of the British Empire, as far-flung colonies asserted independence.

It was first created at the 1926 Imperial Conference, where nations ruled by Britain and those with semi-independent status declared that they were all equal members — not ruled by the United Kingdom — but agreed that they still owed allegiance to the British monarch.

The modern-day Commonwealth dates to 1949, two years after India, Britain’s largest former colony, declared independence from the crown. Meeting in London, the leaders of Britain and other nations agreed to allow membership in the Commonwealth to any country, including those that no longer pledged allegiance to the British king or queen.

Under the London Declaration, the head of the Commonwealth is chosen by its members, rather than inheriting the title. Still, the group’s first leader was King George VI, Charles’s grandfather. He was succeeded upon his death by Queen Elizabeth II, Charles’s mother, and she was succeeded by King Charles. However, in 2022, Prince William, the heir to the British throne, seemed to suggest he might not be the group’s next leader, saying: “Who the Commonwealth chooses to lead its family in the future isn’t what is on my mind.”

There are 56 countries in the Commonwealth now, including four — Mozambique, Rwanda, Gabon and Togo — that were never connected to the British Empire.

Otherwise, it can be divided into two broad groups.

Fourteen nations outside the United Kingdom recognize the British king or queen as their ceremonial head of state, making them, symbolically, subjects of the monarchy. They are not ruled by Britain and they have their own governments. The largest of these are Canada, Australia and New Zealand. Several are in the Caribbean, including Jamaica and the Bahamas.

Forty-one other countries are members without recognizing the British monarch as their head of state. Some have kings or queens of their own. They include nearly two dozen countries in Africa and several in Asia, the Pacific, Europe and the Americas.

At several recent meetings of the Commonwealth, the leaders of some nations have argued that Britain should pay reparations to the descendants of people who were enslaved by the British Empire.

Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, has been one of the loudest voices for reparations, arguing that Britain should be held accountable for the exploitation of slaves. Others have argued that Britain should provide financial reparations to the countries involved, rather than to individuals, as a way of apologizing for its major role in the trans-Atlantic slave trade.

The British government has so far rejected any form of financial reparations or the giving of an official apology. King Charles has acknowledged what he has called the “appalling atrocity of slavery,” but his constitutional role prevents him from diverging from official government policy, meaning he cannot apologize on behalf of Britain unless the government asks him to.

The other ongoing debate among some Commonwealth countries is whether to leave the realm and adopt a republican form of government with no allegiance to the British monarchy.

Prime Minister Gaston Browne of Antigua and Barbuda, where this year’s Commonwealth meeting will be held, said in 2022 that his country should hold a referendum on the issue within three years.

That vote has yet to take place, and the prime minister has said more recently that he is not sure the country is yet ready. The Barbados Parliament voted in 2021 to become a republic, severing its ties with the British crown.

In Jamaica, a bill was introduced in the country’s legislature in 2024 that would shift the country to a republican form of government and cut ties with the monarchy in Britain.

The Commonwealth itself has no formal authority over its member countries. But it does lay out its shared values, typically in a long statement issued at the end of the Commonwealth heads of government meeting — known as “Chogm” — every two years.

After the meeting in Samoa in 2024, it issued a 16-page communiqué, pledging support for world peace, better health care, the environment, the rule of law and human rights.

What the group did not do was weigh in on current events around the world. There was no mention of Ukraine, Russia, Iran or the Middle East, or of most other conflicts around the world.

Critics of the Commonwealth have argued in recent years that its lack of power or authority has rendered it a largely meaningless international institution that should be reformed or even abandoned. Supporters argue that it can be a source of guidance in a volatile world and allows small countries and middle powers access to and communication with larger countries.
