item.title: Jordan Airstrikes on Syria Kill Seven Civilians, Syrian State Media Says
item.description:
Jordan carried out airstrikes on several sites in southern Syria late Monday, killing at least seven civilians, including three children, according to Syrian state media, in an attack that threatened to cool revived diplomatic ties between the two countries.

The Jordanian military, in a statement on social media, said it was “targeting hide-outs of terrorist organizations” in retaliation for an attack on a church in southern Jordan on Friday, which killed nine people. It said the suspects who carried out the attack on the Greek Orthodox Church in the village of Hamoud had ties to the “terrorist organizations” it targeted in the strikes.

It did not identify the groups it was targeting.

Jordan said it had coordinated the operation with the Syrian government beforehand. But the Syrian government said Jordan had carried out the strikes on its territory without prior coordination or notification.

Jordanian military jets struck Syria the same day that its security forces captured three men in Jordan who the authorities say are linked to the church attack, according to state media.

On Friday gunmen emerged from a vehicle and opened fire on the church during a funeral, in what Jordanian officials called a terrorist attack. The attack also left nearly three dozen wounded.

In a statement on Tuesday, the Syrian government stopped short of condemning the strikes, saying it had launched an investigation. The government also said it stood in solidarity with the affected families and would work to give them the necessary support.

“Concurrently, communication channels have been opened with our brothers in the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan to discuss the situation,” the statement said. “We underscore the importance of joint field and security coordination regarding any actions in the border regions, in a manner that preserves the sovereignty of the Syrian Arab Republic and safeguards the security and stability of both brotherly nations.”

Syria’s Foreign Ministry also issued a statement saying it had conveyed its “full reservation” to Jordan for conducting operations inside Syria without coordination and was in communication with its Jordanian counterpart to understand how the strike had happened and “address its repercussions.”

In response to the strikes, Syria’s port authority announced the closure of the Nasib border crossing between southern Syria and Jordan starting on Tuesday “due to prevailing circumstances,” suspending passenger and commercial traffic in both directions.

Diplomatic relations between Syria and Jordan have warmed since the ouster of the Assad regime in Syria in late 2024.

The Jordanian strikes came days after Syria’s foreign minister, Asaad al-Shaibani, met with King Abdullah II of Jordan and other high-level officials to discuss the development of relations between the two countries and coordination on regional developments, including in southern Syria, according to Syrian state media.

Earlier, King Abdullah affirmed his country’s support in preserving Syria’s security and territorial integrity, in light of increasing Israeli attacks and incursions into southern Syria.

Jordanian officials have not said exactly what motivated the shooting at the church, one of the deadliest attacks in Jordan in years, which targeted the country’s small Christian minority. But hours after the attack, Prime Minister Jafar Hassan said that it was “the result of terrorist takfiri ideology,” an Arabic term commonly used to describe Islamist extremists who declare other Muslims heretics.

item.title: Hong Kong’s ‘Apartment Horror’ Films Skewer Its Ghastly Property Market
item.description:
Hong Kong apartments can be terrifying. And it’s not just their price tag.

The city — where a parking spot can fetch more than half a million dollars and some people are forced to live in subdivided accommodation known as “coffin homes” — is one of the least affordable property markets on the planet. This tension has given rise to a subgenre of Hong Kong horror films in which high-density housing is a spooky backdrop for exploring superstition and socioeconomic anxieties.

“In Hong Kong, the ghosts and the spirits are trapped in the apartment with you,” said Roy Tan, a screenwriter and filmmaker in the city. “You can’t get out, and they can’t get out either.”

One “apartment horror” movie, “Coffin Homes” (Fruit Chan, 2021), is a splatter-filled satire that bites into the absurdities of capitalism and the Hong Kong property market. In the film, it is the ghosts who are displeased by the attempts of the living to share their space — a glimpse into a very Hong Kong superstition, where a suspiciously cheap apartment is a sign that it was most likely the site of a tragedy or grisly crime.

The films are steeped in Hong Kong folklore, in which “it is generally believed that the dead live among us all the time,” said Tobias Zuser, a lecturer at the Chinese University of Hong Kong and Hong Kong Baptist University whose courses include discussions on global horror cinema.

“It’s this wonderful contradiction between a hyper-modern city and the persistence of folk beliefs,” he said, adding that this means superstitions are more focused on trying to appease ghosts than denying their existence.

While there is no shortage of spirits in apartment horror films, the real dread often comes when people try to break into the Hong Kong property market — something that “Dream Home” (Pang Ho-cheung, 2010) makes explicit.

The film’s main character spends her whole life working multiple jobs to save up for an apartment, only for the owners to hike up the price at the last minute. That sends her on a prodigiously gory killing spree that, sure enough, ends up lowering the price of homes in the building. As the film says in its ominous opening screed: “In a crazy city, if one is to survive, he’s got to be more crazy.”

Yung-Hang Bruce Lai, a film critic, researcher and programmer from Hong Kong, said that horror films are an effective vector for this brand of social commentary because they illustrate the tension between what you want and what you can’t get, particularly in the city’s housing market. “Anxiety and desire are two sides of the same coin,” he said.

Gary Bettinson, a co-editor of the book “Hong Kong Horror Cinema,” said the source of horror in many films in this subgenre is the place the characters live in or move to.

“It’s not a monster — the monster is the property,” he said.

He added that frequent targets include the government’s struggle to cope with the housing situation, as well as “rapacious and unscrupulous landlords and property developers.”

Hong Kong’s topography gives its horror movies a distinct texture. With little space to build, developers look upward — ensuring a setting with spooky liminal spaces and dizzying verticality. In “Rigor Mortis” (Juno Mak, 2013), a phantasmagoric film with a cast of veteran Hong Kong horror stars, ghoulish apparitions stalk cramped corridors and bloody fights break out in small rooms.

Mr. Tan, the screenwriter, said that the city’s limited housing space is an inspiration for filmmakers. “Around the world, it’s life, death and taxes,” he said. “But in Hong Kong, taxes are so low that it’s life, death and square footage.”

This claustrophobic approach is markedly different from the sprawling haunted houses of many Western horror movies: less a fear of the unknown and more the intimate, immediate dread of what lurks beside you. Elevators are another terrifyingly tight space — used to great effect in “Out of the Dark” (Jeffrey Lau, 1995), a slapstick horror comedy involving attempts to exorcise a haunted apartment building.

And then there are rooftops, often a shared space in Hong Kong apartment buildings. They “become scenes of abjection and horror” when protagonists find themselves on the precipice, “hovering over this abyss and sometimes plunging into it,” said Mr. Bettinson, the “Hong Kong Horror Cinema” editor. Both “Out of the Dark” and “Home Sweet Home” (Soi Cheang, 2005) — in which a mother and son are terrorized in their new apartment by what appears to be a monster — have a climax set on rooftops.

At their most effective, apartment horror films turn the concept of a home on its head by subverting what is meant to be a safe and comfortable environment.

“The home turns against you; it’s a deep-seated fear,” Mr. Bettinson said.

Those fears are often made worse by the constant cacophony of the city. Air-conditioners drip and hum, traffic sounds echo and warp from far below, and the sheer density of living means there is no shortage of mundane things that go bump in the night. Or so we’d like to think.

“Hearing strange noises from time to time is something that every resident in Hong Kong will have to get used to at some point,” said Mr. Zuser, the university lecturer. “We are usually best off telling ourselves that this is either the piping, the neighbor or just the security guard.”

item.title: The Issues Dividing Israelis as They Vote
item.description:
Four years of internal turmoil, war and growing global isolation have left Israelis bitterly divided over their country’s future as they vote in national elections on Tuesday. Opinion polls suggest it will be a close race with the possibility that neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s party nor his opponents will secure a majority.

Many Israelis see the election as choice over whether to continue the rule of the country’s most hard-line, right-wing government ever, and the dominant fault line is Mr. Netanyahu himself. Critics say he has steered Israel to the lowest point in its history, while his supporters see him as an indispensable leader who has tried to destroy Israel’s enemies in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

Beyond Mr. Netanyahu’s leadership, however, there are plenty of issues polarizing the country.

The Hamas-led attacks of Oct. 7, 2023, loom over the vote. About 1,200 Israelis were killed in the assault and 250 were seized as hostages, according to the Israeli authorities, making it the deadliest day in Israeli history. Israel’s military response in Gaza killed more than 70,000 people and led to widespread destruction and displacement of Palestinians.

Three years later, Israelis still have no official answer about why Mr. Netanyahu’s government and the Israeli military failed to foresee the attacks and then struggled to respond even as Hamas fighters invaded villages and a music festival, killing civilians.

Mr. Netanyahu’s opponents — a bloc of opposition parties and their leaders — have said they would establish an independent inquiry with broad authority, appointed by the president of the Supreme Court. Mr. Netanyahu has called for a “democratic and equitable” commission that would be made of an equal number of representatives of the coalition and the opposition.

Families of those killed and taken hostage broadly back the opposition, arguing that Mr. Netanyahu’s proposal would politicize what should be a comprehensive and dispassionate investigation.

Secular and liberal Israelis have long been uneasy about the status of the ultra-Orthodox, an insular community that adheres to a fundamentalist interpretation of Jewish scripture and makes up about 10 percent of the population. Their religious students are eligible for an exemption from mandatory military service and receive state benefits despite not joining the work force.

During the wars in Gaza and Lebanon, that long-simmering frustration boiled over into outrage. Hundreds of Israelis from other backgrounds were killed in combat, and hundreds of thousands more did dangerous rounds of reserve duty.

Mr. Netanyahu’s government has relied heavily on the support of ultra-Orthodox parties. His opponents have called for ending the exemption to the draft for the ultra-Orthodox and cutting off welfare benefits for those who avoid military service.

Before the war, Mr. Netanyahu’s government had sought to advance a highly contentious plan to weaken Israel’s judiciary. Hundreds of thousands of Israelis protested the proposals in mass demonstrations, saying that Mr. Netanyahu was leading the country toward dictatorship.

The Hamas-led attacks largely suspended the overhaul of the courts, part of which was also reversed by a Supreme Court ruling. But Mr. Netanyahu’s allies say they will push ahead with the changes if they are re-elected.

While global attention has focused on the West Bank and Gaza, domestically both Mr. Netanyahu and his opponents have preferred to focus on other issues. Still, they have different visions for the future of these areas.

Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition is dominated by religious nationalists who have advanced Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank at a breakneck pace. They have called for Israel to urge Palestinians to leave Gaza, with one senior minister saying conditions there should be kept miserable to “take away their hope.”

The fractious bloc of parties opposing Mr. Netanyahu hold wildly diverging views on the Palestinians. Gadi Eisenkot, who opinion polls suggest will lead the alliance, has vowed to rein in Israeli extremist attacks on Palestinians and engage on the Trump administration’s cease-fire plan for Gaza.

item.title: 5 Key Moments From Israel’s Pivotal Election Campaign
item.description:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff, have emerged as the top candidates to form the next government in Israel after the general election on Tuesday, the country’s first since the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks set off the war in Gaza.

But other candidates have brought their own drama to the campaign, which has also featured revelations about security failures and a furor over an A.I.-generated political ad.

Here are some key moments from the campaign.

Before Election Day had even been set, the opposition politicians Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, both former prime ministers, announced a joint run for office. The two men have worked together before: They briefly unseated Mr. Netanyahu in 2021, forming a government that lasted less than two years.

Their announcement in April was seen as mutually beneficial, positioning Mr. Bennett as a candidate for prime minister and ensuring that Mr. Lapid would remain one of the most prominent figures in the anti-Netanyahu bloc.

But their ambition to make their unified party, B’Yachad, the largest in the Knesset quickly fizzled. Surveys consistently suggest the party will finish in third place.

Parties across Israel’s political spectrum have published A.I.-generated content to reinforce their messaging. The content has sometimes stirred up controversy — no more so than in July, when Mr. Netanyahu posted a video depicting Mr. Eisenkot.

In the video, Mr. Eisenkot is shown running through a meadow, arms open, toward a man with a striking resemblance to his late son Gal, who was killed in 2023 at the start of the Israeli military’s war in Gaza. But he runs past the young man, instead embracing Mansour Abbas, a prominent Arab politician. Mr. Netanyahu has sought to paint Mr. Abbas, who could help Mr. Eisenkot form a governing coalition, as a supporter of terrorism.

Mr. Netanyahu’s party, Likud, denied that the young man in the video looked like Mr. Eisenkot’s son or was meant to evoke him. But many Israelis reacted to the ad with anger and disgust. Matan Kahana, a former lawmaker running on Mr. Eisenkot’s slate, said there was “no bottom to the pit the Likud is willing to sink into.”

One of the campaign’s most surprising moments came when Mr. Abbas and Yoav Segalovitz, a veteran Zionist politician and former police commander, announced a joint run. Teaming up on the slate of the United Arab List, or Raam, they offered themselves as an example of Jewish-Arab cooperation, even as they braced for intense criticism from both of their communities.

“There are people who are afraid of partnership,” Mr. Abbas said. “There are parties that are afraid of partnership. They are afraid of what people will say, afraid of what they will lose. Raam is not afraid of partnership. Raam advances it.”

Mr. Netanyahu came under new pressure over reports in the Israeli media and in The New York Times that Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed, the president of the United Arab Emirates, had warned him in advance of Oct. 7, 2023, that Hamas was considering a major attack on Israel.

The warning from Sheikh Mohammed never reached the leaders of Israel’s security establishment, The Times reported, citing five former senior Israeli officials. Mr. Netanyahu has denied the reports.

Israelis seemed to forget the election for a day in late September, when the news emerged that a handful of their fellow citizens had stopped a pilot from crashing a FlyDubai commercial jet bound for Tel Aviv.

Mr. Netanyahu spent hours celebrating the passengers’ resourcefulness, diverting attention away from headlines at the time about his and other officials’ failure to stop the Hamas-led attack in 2023.

Within days, however, his government was on the defensive over revelations of security failures that had allowed the FlyDubai pilot, an Omani man said to have embraced extreme Islamist views, into the cockpit in the first place.

item.title: Jordan Arrests 3 in Connection With Church Attack, State Media Reports
item.description:
Jordanian security forces arrested three men early Monday accused of carrying out an attack last week during a funeral at a church in southern Jordan that killed nine people, according to state media.

Security and commando forces captured the three suspects during a predawn raid on their hide-out in an abandoned house in Karak, the same southern province where the attack on a Greek Orthodox Church took place, according to Petra, the Jordanian state media service.

It said the suspects refused orders to surrender and opened fire, so the security forces responded in kind — wounding and disarming the three men before taking them into custody.

No security personnel were injured in the raid, Petra reported, adding that guns and ammunition were found inside the hide-out.

The suspects were not identified, and the authorities have not released details about what charges they will face.

The shooting in the village of Hamoud in southern Jordan was one of the deadliest attacks in the country in years.

Officials have not said exactly what motivated the deadly assault, which they called a terrorist attack. Prime Minister Jafar Hassan said at a news conference on Friday that it was “the result of terrorist takfiri ideology,” an Arabic term commonly used to describe Islamist extremists who declare other Muslims heretics.

“We have apprehended the killers, we are examining every factor that leads youth toward extremism, and we will hold accountable anyone proven to have been involved,” Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya wrote on social media on Monday.

The attack on Friday, which also injured nearly three dozen people, was met with widespread condemnation across Jordan. Officials vowed it would not divide Jordanians or threaten national stability.

King Abdullah II, who has ruled the kingdom through more than a quarter-century of regional upheaval, said on Friday that the attackers would be met with “the harshest retaliation.”

While Christians make up only about 2 percent of Jordan’s population, the country is home to some of the most important biblical and Christian pilgrimage sites, including what is said to be the location where Jesus was baptized. Christian Jordanians are guaranteed seats in Parliament and have long served as cabinet ministers and ambassadors.

The Christian presence in Karak dates back more than 1,500 years, to a time when the Eastern Roman Empire ruled that part of the Middle East.

Jordan, a close U.S. ally, has largely avoided the violence that has destabilized many of its neighbors, though it has faced sporadic militant attacks over the past decade. In 2016, Islamic State militants killed 10 people in a shooting rampage in and around the city of Karak before taking shelter in a medieval castle there.

item.title: Norway Pushes Back After Trump Disparages It Over Nobel Prize Decision
item.description:
President Trump was courteous toward Norway during his first term, describing it as a country the United States should accept more immigrants from. But on Sunday, two weeks after the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded its 2026 Peace Prize, he disparaged the country using a vulgar term for an outhouse.

“Frankly, Norway sucks,” Mr. Trump said at a campaign rally in Port Huron, Mich., on Sunday. “Norway has become a shithouse country, actually.”

He suggested that the United States should accept fewer Norwegian immigrants, saying, “I didn’t get the Nobel Prize.”

“So I don’t want anybody from Norway,” the president continued. “I don’t want anything to do with Norway.”

The Nobel Peace Prize — which the president has openly campaigned for — was awarded in Oslo to Navi Pillay, a South African human rights lawyer.

Mr. Trump’s remarks were met with bewilderment and exasperation in Norway, where top government officials have repeatedly said that they do not have influence over who is awarded the Peace Prize.

“He knows very well that the Nobel committee is independent,” Espen Barth Eide, the Norwegian foreign minister, told the country’s public broadcaster NRK on Monday. “We have reminded him of that, in case anyone is wondering, and that is still the case.”

Norwegians on social media expressed their dismay at Mr. Trump’s remarks, although few seemed surprised. Some pointed out that Mr. Trump had described Norway in 2018 in glowing terms that were racially tinged when he contrasted the country with Haiti.

Norwegians generally view Mr. Trump’s public comments with some skepticism, said Eirik Lokke, an analyst at Civita, a centrist think tank in Oslo.

“We have simply grown accustomed to his erratic behavior and tend not to take every outburst too seriously,” he said.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee said in a statement on Monday that it was “entirely independent of the Norwegian government.”

Norway’s Parliament appoints the committee’s five members for six-year terms. To protect the organization’s independence, members of the government have been barred from sitting on the committee since 1936 and incumbent lawmakers since 1977.

Mr. Trump has openly jockeyed for the Peace Prize for about a decade, mentioning it in dozens of interviews and speeches and also complaining about it privately. He described the committee’s decision this month to award Ms. Pillay the 2026 prize as “an indelible stain on Norway.”

In its announcement on Oct. 9, the Nobel committee said it was honoring Ms. Pillay, 85, for her efforts to promote international law. Over the years, she served as a top U.N. official and a judge on the International Criminal Court. Last year, she led a U.N. commission on Israel that said it was committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, a finding that Israel rejected.

At the rally on Sunday in Michigan, where the Trump ally Mike Rogers is locked in a close Senate contest with the Democrat Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the president returned again to the subject of the Nobel Prize, indicating that he had expected to be awarded it while also suggesting he had been too busy to give the issue much attention.

He repeated his claim that he had settled eight wars, which he has previously suggested should be rewarded with eight Nobel Peace Prizes. Several of the wars he has previously cited, including those between Israel and Hamas and between Israel and Iran, remain unresolved.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.

item.title: Flurry of Diplomacy in Iran as Regional Countries Try to Stave Off War
item.description:
Senior representatives from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met with Iranian officials in the capital, Tehran, on Monday, amid widespread concern that the United States and Israel could soon launch fresh attacks on Iran.

Ali Bagheri Kani, the deputy secretary of Iran’s powerful Supreme National Security Council, said the meetings were aimed at promoting regional security, according to an Iranian state news channel, Press TV.

The visit is the latest in a flurry of diplomatic efforts by regional mediators to stave off further turmoil in the Middle East. American and Israeli officials are said to be drawing up plans to potentially attack Iran after the U.S. midterm elections next week, according to U.S. officials and others briefed on the deliberations.

Saudi Arabia’s conflict with the Iranian-backed Houthi militia in Yemen has also escalated rapidly in recent weeks as the two sides have exchanged deadly attacks, including on airports and oil sites around the kingdom.

Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan formed a new collective defense agreement, known as the Mecca Pact, this year. Monday’s talks are their first joint high-level meeting with Iran since the Saudi-Houthi conflict flared up.

The Saudi defense minister, Prince Khalid bin Salman, is representing the kingdom in the talks, according to a statement from Saudi Arabia’s foreign ministry. The prince is joined in Tehran by Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, Iranian state media said, as well as Ibrahim Kalin, head of the Turkish national intelligence agency.

On Monday afternoon, Iran’s state broadcaster reported that the officials were meeting with Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, and the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei.

A day earlier, Qatari mediators visited Tehran to try to hammer out an agreement between the United States and Iran and stave off renewed regional war, according to Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman, Esmaeil Baghaei. Last week, Mr. Munir of Pakistan also made a visit to Tehran to help in diplomatic efforts.

A Gulf official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the negotiations, said the talks on Monday were supporting the efforts of Qatari and Pakistani mediators and were intended, in part, to urge Iran to show enough flexibility to reach a diplomatic solution with the United States.

Qatari mediators have been working on an agreement between the United States and Iran in which the two sides would make a series of concessions over a five-day period, two diplomats briefed on the talks said.

They said that, as part of the concessions, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for energy shipping in the Persian Gulf, for commercial shipping, while the United States would lift a naval blockade on Iran’s ports that has deepened the country’s economic crisis.

The main stumbling block to that agreement has been determining when each side would make its concessions, the diplomats said. They added that the mediators have been pushing for Iran to offer a concession on its nuclear program in the initial phase of the agreement.

Iran has repeatedly ruled out giving up part of its enriched uranium stockpile, and last week, Mr. Rezaei vowed that “not a single particle of enriched nuclear material” would leave Iran.

Iranian officials last week signaled pessimism that an agreement could be reached and warned that if Iran were attacked again, its forces would expand their targets to data centers and underwater internet cables in the region.

The visit by senior Saudi officials to Tehran is a significant outreach at a time of profound tensions between the two countries, as Saudi Arabia contends with near-daily attacks by the Iranian-backed Houthis.

Sending Prince Khalid — the brother and trusted envoy of the kingdom’s crown prince — would appear to suggest that the Saudi leadership is intent on avoiding another round of war between the U.S., Israel and Iran, which could bring a fresh barrage of Iranian attacks on Saudi Arabia while it is also battling the Houthis.

For Iran, the visit by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan on Monday is symbolically significant, as Iranian officials are eager to sideline the United States from regional security and diplomatic arrangements.

The Mecca Pact was signed in August as countries in the Middle East have sought new ways to ensure their security amid uncertainty about the reliability of American protection. That has become particularly important to leaders in the Gulf Arab countries, which faced a barrage of Iranian missiles and drones after the U.S. and Israeli attack began in February.

“From our perspective, the very fact that regional countries are seeking to establish, or at least contemplate, regional security mechanisms based on their own interests and considerations is a welcome development,” Mr. Baghaei, the Iranian foreign ministry spokesman, said at a news conference in Tehran on Monday.

Aaron Boxerman and Sanam Mahoozi contributed reporting.

item.title: Lula Wins Brazil’s Presidency, in Stunning Blow to Latin America’s Right
item.description:
Brazilian voters on Sunday handed the leftist president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a fourth term in office and a surprise victory over Flávio Bolsonaro, his right-wing challenger, in a striking rebuke to a conservative surge sweeping Latin America.

Mr. Bolsonaro refused to accept the outcome and said it was the result of foul play, increasing the risk of unrest over the election result.

The rejection by voters of Mr. Bolsonaro, the son of a former president jailed for attempting a coup four years ago, is also a loss for President Trump, who had embraced the Bolsonaro family and the region’s rising right.

Mr. Lula, in contrast to many world leaders, has often and defiantly clashed with Mr. Trump, and his victory suggests that Latin America’s left-wing forces still wield influence despite a string of losses across the hemisphere. This is the first leftist victory following seven straight wins by right-wing leaders in the region over the last 18 months.

“I would like to thank the Brazilian people for the generosity they have shown me for a long time,” Mr. Lula said, during a victory speech in São Paulo, flanked by his wife, running mate and allies.

The result capped a chaotic final stretch of the race, as polling places were ordered to remain open after public transportation delays and torrential rains disrupted voting. The extended polling hours, which both candidates asked for but came right as voting was set to conclude, opened up the possibility that the results would be disputed.

Mr. Bolsonaro called an order by Brazil’s judiciary to extend voting a “dirty trick” and demanded the election be annulled.

“There’s a lot that needs to be cleared up before Brazil simply accepts this foul play that took place in these elections,” he said during a news conference in Brasília, the capital.

Mr. Bolsonaro’s party will now likely petition electoral authorities for a review of the result.

Since Brazil’s return to democracy, no presidential election has ever been annulled. In 2014, the losing party requested an audit, but that review found no evidence of fraud and the results were upheld.

In 2022, Mr. Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party similarly challenged his father’s loss in the election, but the court ultimately fined the party more than $4 million for failing to provide evidence to support its allegations.

Among Mr. Bolsonaro’s supporters on Sunday, the sentiment was one of sadness and indignation. “We know we’ve been robbed again,” said Valéria Maria de Melo, a 49-year-old housewife, bursting into tears.

Mr. Lula headed into Sunday’s vote as the underdog after finishing 2 percentage points behind his opponent in the first round of voting earlier this month.

But on Sunday, Mr. Lula achieved a stunning comeback, winning 51.8 percent of the vote versus 48.2 percent for Flávio Bolsonaro, with nearly all the ballots counted.

Mr. Lula’s margin of victory on Sunday was roughly double the margin four years ago when he narrowly defeated Mr. Bolsonaro’s father. It was the first time in Brazil’s history that a candidate who lost the first round of voting came back to win the second.

Mr. Lula’s victory was even more surprising given that several of the candidates who failed to make it out of the first round were conservatives whose votes were expected to broadly shift to Mr. Bolsonaro.

Mr. Lula, speaking at a hotel surrounded by cheering allies and supporters, thanked those who had voted for him. In an indirect swipe at Mr. Trump, he said the mass rallies in Brazilian cities in the days leading up to the vote were “a demonstration that this country refuses to be anyone’s backyard.”

“I want to thank the generosity of the Brazilian youth, who took to the streets to defend democracy,” he added.

The results suggested that far more voters had turned up to cast a ballot on Sunday than in the earlier round, a highly unusual shift. Typically, the number of voters drops from the first round to the second. In total, more than 128 million Brazilians voted on Sunday, compared to 125 million in the first round.

An intense social media campaign that included a wildly popular channel on WhatsApp, a platform long dominated by Mr. Bolsonaro’s right-wing movement, played a major role in mobilizing Mr. Lula’s supporters in the final stretch of the race.

As he celebrated in Rio de Janeiro, Fernando Porto said he and his friends never gave up hope as they took to social media and to the streets to rally support for Mr. Lula over the last three weeks. “This comeback was truly incredible,” said Mr. Porto, 24, a psychology student.

In São Paulo, a massive celebration that had already erupted long before the results came grew quickly with news of Mr. Lula’s victory. Supporters of the president broke down in tears of disbelief and set off fireworks, while cars honked in a deafening chorus of horns.

Mr. Lula’s comeback win capped a roller-coaster career for the president that has traversed soaring popularity, scandal and prison, and now an election that deeply divided Brazil, forcing voters to choose between two starkly different visions for the future of Latin America’s largest nation.

A stalwart of Brazilian politics, Mr. Lula lifted millions out of poverty through social programs in earlier years as president, though his popularity waned in his third term as he failed to address anxieties over crime and the economy.

His political legacy has also been tarnished by links to corruption scandals, including a new one unfolding on his watch that has implicated much of Brazil’s political and judicial elite, including Mr. Bolsonaro himself.

Yet Sunday’s narrow tally makes clear that Mr. Lula, 80, faces a daunting task: leading a polarized nation plagued by a spiraling debt crisis, high grocery prices and growing fears about organized crime. And Mr. Lula is bound to face resistance at every turn, after voters elected an overwhelming number of Mr. Bolsonaro’s political allies to the Legislature.

And the strong showing of Mr. Bolsonaro, 45, highlights that the right-wing leader’s ideas resonate with millions of working-class Brazilians who may have supported Mr. Lula in the past, but have become disillusioned with him.

Ultimately, though, a majority of voters appears to have heeded Mr. Lula’s warnings about handing power to another Bolsonaro, just four years after former President Jair Bolsonaro orchestrated a plan to hold onto the presidency and inspired supporters to storm Brazil’s halls of power.

Last year, the elder Mr. Bolsonaro was sentenced to 27 years in prison for trying to stage a coup after the 2022 election, in a plot that included plans to assassinate Mr. Lula, Mr. Lula’s running mate and a Supreme Court justice.

The younger Mr. Bolsonaro had said he planned to seek amnesty for his father and the rioters, impeach the Supreme Court justice who oversaw their jailing, and change the nation’s constitution.

Mr. Lula’s resounding win on Sunday signals that the majority of Brazilians want to protect their democracy, said Christian Lynch, a political scientist at the State University of Rio de Janeiro.

“People here realized they don’t want to surrender democracy,” he said. “It was a big surprise.”

Mr. Lula’s win will most likely complicate Mr. Trump’s plans for dominance in the region: The Brazilian leader has repeatedly defied Mr. Trump over issues like trade, social media and the treatment of the Bolsonaros.

Mr. Trump remained silent about Mr. Lula’s win on Sunday. While he had not formally endorsed Mr. Bolsonaro, his administration had appeared willing to help him in other ways, such as by labeling Brazil’s largest drug gangs as terror groups. Last year, the American president also tried, and failed, to help Mr. Bolsonaro’s father avoid jail by hitting Brazil with tariffs and sanctions.

Turning Brazilian sovereignty into a rallying cry, Mr. Lula repeatedly urged voters to reject the younger Mr. Bolsonaro, painting him as a puppet of the United States.

Sunday’s result signaled that many Brazilians had rejected Mr. Bolsonaro’s cozy ties with the United States.

Despite Mr. Lula’s disagreements with Mr. Trump, Brazil’s economy was largely unscathed by American tariffs during his third term, and unemployment dropped to record-low rates. But rising food prices and mounting household debt have weighed heavily on Mr. Lula’s approval ratings.

Many Brazilians are also eager to see if Mr. Lula makes good on his promises for a judicial overhaul amid a crisis of confidence in Brazil’s top court. The next president will have unusually broad power to shape the court, which has 11 members, by filling up to four seats freed by justices reaching the mandatory retirement age.

“Most people want change,” said Thomas Traumann, a political analyst and press secretary for a former leftist Brazilian president, “but not the Bolsonaro change.”

Reporting was contributed by Giovana Sanchez in São Paulo; Thayz Guimarães in Brasília; Silvia Ribeiro, Leonardo Coelho, Isabela Cruz and Lis Moriconi in Rio de Janeiro; Naira Hofmeister in Pôrto Alegre.

item.title: Serbia’s Election Shows New Vulnerability for Nationalist Populists
item.description:
When voters in Hungary rejected their seemingly invincible populist leader Viktor Orban in April, Andrej Borovac, a young designer in neighboring Serbia, was ecstatic, but he was downbeat about his own country’s populist strongman suffering the same fate.

“That can never happen here,” he recalled thinking. Aleksandar Vucic, Serbia’s dominant political figure since 2012, looked immovable, given his grip — established over more than a decade in power — on security forces, nearly all major media outlets, the electoral commission and many other institutions. Or so he thought.

On Sunday night, Mr. Borovac, 38, and two friends joined tens of thousands of people gathered near Parliament in Belgrade, the Serbian capital, to celebrate Mr. Vucic’s defeat in a pivotal election for a new legislature.

“The Hungarian Spring has come to Serbia in the fall,” Mr. Borovac said late Sunday night, surrounded by revelers waving Serbian flags and setting off red flares. Nearby, a group of young Serbs danced for joy.

At a time of rising liberal fears of surging support for right-wing nationalists, the formerly Communist East, an early pioneer of populist politics after the collapse of Soviet hegemony in 1989, is showing that tides can turn.

Elections this year in Hungary and Serbia, and in Poland in 2023, have given new life to mostly forgotten liberal hopes voiced in “The Power of the Powerless,” a 1978 book by Vaclav Havel, the Czech dissident who would later become president and a global icon for believers in liberal democracy.

Anger at rampant corruption helped glue together disparate and sometimes contradictory political forces, allowing them to campaign on an issue that resonated with a wider population upset by the conspicuous wealth of people connected to the governing party.

In Germany, France and Italy and elsewhere in Western Europe, the anti-establishment nationalist camp has taken on the appearance of an invincible juggernaut, and it may yet show strongly in a raft of elections next year. But for the moment, in Eastern Europe and beyond, it is newly showing signs of strain.

On the same day as Serbia’s election, voters in Brazil narrowly rejected an all but preordained victory for the hard right and handed a win to the leftist president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

The Serbian election will also add to the discomfit of President Trump’s MAGA movement, which for now lags in many polls ahead of what is expected to be a difficult election next week. It had looked to the Serbian leader as a kindred spirit committed to defending national sovereignty and resisting European liberals. Mr. Trump’s family eyed it for business deals.

A few weeks before the election, the Conservative Political Action Conference, or CPAC, a MAGA-aligned American organization, announced that it would hold its first gathering in the Balkan region, to be held in Belgrade in November and “headlined by President Aleksandar Vucic.”

CPAC had previously focused its European activities on Hungary, where it held a big annual gathering, now in doubt following Mr. Orban’s defeat and the end of state funding by the new government to foundations that helped bankroll various ventures by “anti-woke” warriors from abroad.

Even in Eastern Europe, the momentum has not been all one-way, and it often zigzags. Parliamentary elections in Slovenia this year and the Czech Republic last year as well as a presidential vote in Poland all saw nationalist forces prevail, albeit by tiny margins.

Also, the forces that have proved ascendant against the nationalist right are themselves a mixed bag that are far from being liberal globalists. Mr. Orban was defeated by a new party led by Peter Magyar, a conservative former Orban loyalist, and Mr. Vucic by a slate of student-selected candidates, nearly all newcomers to politics.

Thorsten Benner, director of the Global Public Policy Institute in Berlin, said the lesson from both Hungary and Serbia was that “at some point, anti-incumbency bias or rage hits these authoritarians,” though the alternative “won’t be picture-perfect liberals.”

“The real positive lesson,” he added “is that these authoritarians can actually lose elections and concede defeat.”

The political party that underpinned Mr. Vucic’s long ascendancy is called the Serbian Progressive Party, hardly a right-wing outfit. It has railed against privatization and vowed to keep big chunks of the economy, which has grown robustly, under state control.

After a record turnout of nearly 70 percent, his party won 39 percent of the vote compared with 52 percent for its main opponent, a new political grouping that emerged from nearly two years of student-led protest called Student List-Students Win.

The Student List has itself embraced nationalist themes. Many of the people rejoicing Sunday night on the street flashed the three-finger Serbian salute, a patriotic gesture used by marauding ethnic Serb troops during the Balkan wars of the 1990s.

Miljana Pejic, 33, a youth trainer who joined Sunday night’s street celebrations, said the salute in its current use was not a throwback to dark nationalist passions but a “reclaiming and reframing of Serb symbols” that had been hijacked.

“We love our country so perhaps we are nationalist,” she said, “But everything the students advocate — the rule of law, anti-corruption, independent institutions — is in line with the values of the European Union,” she said.

Serbia applied to join the European bloc in 2009, but its application largely stalled under Mr. Vucic, whose brand of nationalism and illiberal politics closely resembled that of his ally Mr. Orban in Hungary.

In the end, both men nonetheless conceded defeat when it became obvious that the groundswell of discontent from voters had overwhelmed their best, years-old attempts to tilt the political playing field their way, not least by manipulating the media.

In an early concession speech Sunday evening, Mr. Vucic lamented that “they toppled us,” blaming his defeat on shadowy foreign forces. The election result, he said, “was the verification of a revolution carried out with direct support from various European countries and the American deep state — the one opposed to President Trump.”

But his biggest problem, as was Mr. Orban’s, was that the election largely became a referendum on himself: he had stopped being popular and, accused of ties to gangsters, become instead a hate figure for large segments of the population, no matter what their political orientations.

Dimitar Bechev, a senior fellow at Carnegie Europe and an expert on the Balkans, said he was surprised by the opposition’s wide margin of victory but added: “You overstay your welcome after many years.”

In both Hungary and Serbia, he said, “when you have a strongman figure, you have a coalition from liberals to people on the far right fed up.”

Bozo Prelevic, an opposition-aligned lawyer, on Monday compared Mr. Vucic to a malignant tumor. “Serbia has freed itself after a long and serious illness, a cancer that was destroying both society and the state, setting citizens against one another and invoking war,” he told N1, an opposition-friendly television channel.

It is unclear what the Student List’s victorious candidates want to do in terms of policy once they take their seats in a new Parliament, which must convene within 30 days of the announcement of the final results. Their campaign revolved around a single issue: getting rid of Mr. Vucic and uprooting what they called his corrupt “mafia.”

The slate of candidates selected by student activists includes no students and comprises academics, musicians, activists, actors, athletes and others from a wide range of backgrounds. Most have no experience in politics or government.

The first candidate on the list was Ilija Srdanovic, a cardiologist from the city of Novi Sad, but he is not the head of a hierarchical party with power to set policy and tell fellow Student List members of Parliament what to do.

In his first public remarks after the election, Mr. Srdanovic chided those who had questioned whether such an amorphous political movement could defeat Mr. Vucic.

“We believed not just in victory, but in a victory so clear that it could not be concealed,” he told RT Balkan, a Russian state-funded news outlet aimed at Serbia.

Alisa Dogramadzieva contributed reporting from Belgrade, and Steven Erlanger from Berlin.

item.title: Egypt Approves Sending Military Support to Defend Saudi Arabia From Houthis
item.description:
Egypt’s Parliament authorized the country’s military on Monday to provide support to Saudi Arabia in its escalating war against the Iranian-backed Houthi militia, Egyptian state media said.

The move, requested by President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi last week, risks drawing the Arab world’s most populous nation deeper into regional turmoil at a time when U.S. and Israeli officials are said to be drawing up plans for renewed attacks on Iran.

Egyptian officials have stressed that the military support will be purely defensive. Mr. el-Sisi said last week that Egyptian forces would operate only inside Saudi borders, and would not be involved in direct attacks on Houthi targets in Yemen, according to state news media.

In a statement, the Parliament said that the military support was aimed at “defending the kingdom’s territory, sovereignty and holy sites against any external aggression.”

Saudi Arabia has not commented on the Egyptian Parliament’s decision, and neither country has publicly confirmed a Saudi request for Egyptian military assistance. The kingdom has in recent weeks exchanged increasingly deadly strikes with the Houthis, who have hit Saudi airports and oil sites.

As the conflict escalated, President Trump rebuffed Saudi appeals last month to launch U.S. strikes against the Houthis. But the United States is providing significant military support, including intelligence in support of the kingdom’s Yemeni allies and refueling for Saudi warplanes conducting defensive air patrols, according to one current and one former U.S. official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters. And last week, the British government said it would send fighter jets to help defend Saudi Arabia’s cities and critical infrastructure.

Egypt had long sought to stay out of rising regional tensions, and to instead support diplomatic initiatives to end the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. That position may have become less tenable as the Saudi-Houthi conflict began threatening shipping through the Red Sea, a vital waterway for global trade that feeds into Egypt’s Suez Canal.

Saudi Arabia is also an important regional ally for Egypt and an important economic backer. Hundreds of thousands of Egyptians work in the kingdom and send remittances back home.

“Egypt can’t afford to let Saudi descend into deeper instability,” said H.A. Hellyer, a senior associate fellow focused on Middle East security at the Royal United Services Institute, a London-based research center. “From Egypt’s point of view, it is reliant on Saudi Arabia being a strong linchpin of the regional security order.”

The decision to send forces to Saudi Arabia is nonetheless fraught for Egyptians, who have not forgotten Egypt’s long and costly involvement in Yemen’s civil war of the 1960s, when tens of thousands of troops were deployed in the country.

Critics have since argued that it severely drained Egypt’s finances and military preparedness for its 1967 war with Israel, when Israel seized the Sinai Peninsula and occupied it for over a decade.

On Monday, with the Parliament expected to make a decision on whether to commit military support, Egypt’s pound hit record lows against the dollar.

Though it remains unclear how many troops Egypt will send to Saudi Arabia, the decision is nonetheless a symbolic boost for the kingdom as it seeks to garner regional and international support.

Egypt’s Parliament began debating the authorization in two closed-door sessions last week at Mr. el-Sisi’s request. The final vote on Monday required at least two-thirds of lawmakers to endorse the decision.

Earlier this month, Egypt’s National Defense Council, whose chairman is Mr. el-Sisi, said that Egypt would provide “all necessary and possible forms of support” to defend the kingdom but did not specify what that would entail.

When Saudi Arabia led a yearslong military intervention against the Houthis in 2015, after the militia seized control of the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, Egypt contributed air and naval support. Egyptian warships also helped protect shipping through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the southern entrance to the Red Sea.

In recent months, that strait has again become a point of contention.

In July, the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, firing on passing tankers. Then last month, they staged a lightning advance along Yemen’s coast, seizing territory adjacent to the Bab al-Mandab from the internationally recognized Yemeni government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.

The threat to Red Sea shipping is of critical concern to Egypt. The Suez Canal is a major source of foreign currency. Yet some Egyptians remain wary of the decision to send forces to fight another Arab force, particularly as it risks embroiling their country in the broader regional conflict.

One lawmaker, Abdel-Alim Dawood, told an Egyptian newspaper, Al-Masry Al-Youm, that he declined to vote, fearing “an explosion in the region that would serve Israel’s interests.”
